stories.title: Apec summit live: Xi and Putin start talks; Rubio says Trump serious about meeting Kim Jong-un
stories.summary: Summit in Chinese tech hub Shenzhen set to include highly anticipated meeting between Xi, Trump and Putin Shenzhen takes centre stage as Xi sends ‘Chinamaxxing’ message at Apec summit What is Apec? Explained in 30 seconds Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up? That is the question the Guardian’s diplomatic correspondent Patrick Wintour seeks to address in his piece about the expected, Putin, Trump and Xi, meeting at Apec on Thursday. stories.body:
Interim summary

Thanks for tuning into our live blog of Apec summit currently under way in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.

There is plenty more to come, so don’t go away, but here is a quick summary of what we know so far.

Chinese president Xi Jinping opened the Apec CEO summit on Wednesday with a speech calling for freer trade and greater cooperation around AI . “We should not only eliminate trade and investment barriers... but also promote inclusive and balanced development,” he said. “We should actively build partnerships for scientific and technological innovation, deepen cooperation in the digital economy and artificial intelligence and promote a green and low-carbon transition.”

Russian president Vladimir Putin also addressed the summit, speaking after Ukraine destroyed the vital Kerch road bridge linking occupied Crimea to Russia in a major blow to his four-year-old war. Putin followed Xi on stage with a speech that described Western powers as “ former hegemons ”. He said Europe was in a “humiliating decline” and that anti-Russian sanctions imposed ⁠after his invasion of Ukraine had backfired, instead making his country stronger.

Xi and Putin headed into a meeting after their opening addresses, according to Chinese and Russian state media.

The much-anticipated trilateral meeting between US president Donald Trump, Xi and Putin will take place on Thursday. The three men are due to meet on the sidelines and potentially discuss Russia’s war with Ukraine and the US war in Iran, as well as other flashpoints such as trade, ⁠AI and nuclear weapons.

The meeting has drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference between the US, Britain and the Soviet Union that formalised spheres of influence , set the stage for world order after the second world war and became shorthand for great power deals imposed on smaller countries.

It is unclear whether North Korean leader Kim Jong-un will attend the talks, but Trump has floated the possibility. On Wednesday US secretary of state Marco Rubio said the US president was willing to engage, but he did not confirm whether a meeting had been set in Shenzhen.

Trump said on Wednesday that the US has just ⁠concluded a “ very big ⁠trade ​deal” with the Philippines , but he did not provide any details, and Manila ⁠did not announce any agreement. “We’ve just consummated a very big trade deal, the ⁠biggest trade deal we’ve ever made so far, and it ​is a fair ‌deal for both countries,” ‌Trump said during a state luncheon at the Philippine ‌presidential palace. Trump is set to arrive in Shenzhen on Wednesday evening.

The looming questions about AI

Donald Trump has said he doesn’t want to talk about Nvidia, the AI giant at the centre of a global espionage scandal, but AI will surely be on the agenda .

Countries have called for stronger governance and regulation of AI , as worries grow about its potential for military use and the risks posed by rogue autonomous-agent tools.

The China-US talks could build on the AI “communication channel” agreed when Trump and Xi met in Washington in September, Reuters reports.

double quotation mark The next step should be to agree on what constitutes a reportable incident, who has authority to communicate, how quickly notifications must occur and how information can be verified without disclosing sensitive capabilities,” said Marina Zhang from the University of Technology Sydney.

Media reports have also suggested Xi, Putin and Trump may discuss the use of AI in nuclear weapons command systems.

Trump’s predecessor Joe Biden and Xi had agreed in 2024 that any decision to use nuclear weapons should be controlled by humans, not by AI, the White House said.

Taiwan sends representative to Apec summit

Taiwan’s representative Stan Shih, founder of computer manufacturer Acer, is expected to arrive in Shenzhen with a delegation this morning.

Among the 21 Apec member economies, Taiwan’s participation is particularly sensitive , given that host country China claims the self-governing democracy as its territory.

Taiwan joined Apec in 1991 under the name “Chinese Taipei” and remains a full member despite its limited diplomatic recognition . Home to TSMC, the world’s leading contract chipmaker, the island plays a crucial role in the global supply of advanced semiconductors essential to AI, a key focus of discussions at the summit.

Ahead of the summit, China reiterated that Taiwan’s participation in Apec must adhere to its “one-China principle”, a position rejected by Taipei, which insists that its participation as a forum member is not subject to Beijing’s policy.

A Tuesday poll show s that 71.8% of respondents in Taiwan supported the government’s participation in the Shenzhen summit on “equal and dignified terms.”

Taiwan could also come up in talks between US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the summit on Thursday.

Asked on Tuesday whether Taiwan had communicated with Washington ahead of Trump’s talks with Chinese and Russian leaders, Taiwan’s foreign ministry spokesperson said communication channels with the US are “running smoothly” and the ministry is closely monitoring Trump’s meetings at the summit.

Apec and trade

Trade tensions are likely to loom over the Apec summit this year, just a year after Trump and Xi Jinping reached a tenuous truce in their trade war on the sidelines of the last Apec summit in South Korea.

But that deal expires in January.

The leaders’ “priority” would be “ keeping the truce alive ”, especially with another Trump-Xi meeting expected at the G20 summit in Miami in December, said Lizzi Lee, a fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI), as reported by Reuters.

Countries like Canada are also expected to be looking to broaden their trade partnerships – including with China – to reduce dependence on the United States.

Trump has of course upended global trade order by imposing wide-ranging tariffs on many countries.

Kim Jong-un had plenty to gain from his three meetings with Donald Trump during the US president’s first term in office .

Seven years on from their last meeting, along the heavily armed border dividing the Korean peninsula, speculation is mounting that the North Korean leader will end their estrangement at this week’s Apec summit in Shenzhen.

But some analysts are casting doubt on the likelihood of a fourth Trump-Kim meeting in the Chinese city.

After making rapid progress with his country’s nuclear and missile programmes and forming a loose “axis of upheaval” with Beijing and Moscow, what, they ask, would Kim have to gain from another encounter with his American counterpart?

Apec’s Chinese hosts say they have no information on a possible bilateral, while the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, appeared to play down the prospect, saying preparations for a dialogue between Kim and Trump did not mean it would happen.

Trump, who floated the idea just before leaving Washington on Monday, has raised the prospect of a resumption of nuclear diplomacy before, yet the men have not met since their brief meeting along the DMZ in June 2019, months after they failed to agree on how US would compensate Pyongyang for dismantling its nuclear arsenal.

Speculation that Kim would make an appearance alongside other world leaders increased, however, after a report by Russia’s Interfax news agency quoted the Kremlin as saying Vladimir Putin could meet Kim ⁠if he attended the Apec summit.

The Kremlin “wouldn’t do that unless they were certain he was going to meet”, Sydney Seiler, a former US national intelligence officer for North Korea, now at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told Reuters. “I’m pretty confident something’s underway.”

Others North Korea experts were more skeptical. Kim would have nothing to gain from a trip to Shenzhen except photo opportunities, said Kim Dong-yup, a professor at Kyungnam University’s Far East Institute. “Let’s say they offer to remove sanctions. But sanctions are already not working. There’s nothing to gain for Kim. Why would he go and open himself up to potential uncertainty?”

North Korean state media have been silent on the speculation. Official photos released this week showed a smiling Kim, accompanied by his wife and daughter, perched on an armchair in the snow at a ski resort near the North Korea-China border.

Wearing aviator shades, a cigarette dangling from his fingers, Kim did not give the impression he was ready to resurrect his “friendship” with a weakened US president.

The Ukraine question

As mentioned earlier, Zelenskyy is undeniably concerned about the Apec trilateral meeting between the Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin .

Ukraine’s foreign minister Andriy Sybiga said earlier this week that a meeting between US, Chinese and Russian leaders would “only encourage Putin to continue this war” .

Beijing has said the three leaders will discuss “safeguarding world peace”, but US officials say Trump is not expected to bring up Russia’s war in Ukraine.

Beijing, insisting it is a neutral party, has never denounced the Russian invasion, and has instead called for peace talks.

“Beijing will remain respectful of Russia’s own aims in the war and balance that with growing calls from Europe to exert a little more influence in that regard,” NTU’s Loh said, as reported by Reuters news agency.

Putin would probably have the most to gain from the trilateral meeting, ASPI’s Lee added.

double quotation mark Just being at the table with Trump and Xi would elevate Russia’s standing and potentially shift the conversation toward a broader great-power bargain over European security.

On the Apec-Yalta comparison

Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up?

That is the question the Guardian’s diplomatic correspondent Patrick Wintour seeks to address in his piece about the expected, Putin, Trump and Xi, meeting at Apec on Thursday.

Some have likened the impending trilateral (pictured below) to the 1945 meeting between Stalin, Churchill and Roosevelt that that in effect carved up postwar Europe, between a communist-ruled east and a democratic, capitalist west.

Among those concerned about the meeting, he writes, is Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy .

double quotation mark It is a truism in diplomacy that if you are not around the table, the risk is that you, or your values, are on the menu and about to be carved up. Many excluded from the summit in Shenzhen, principally Ukraine but also eastern Europe and Baltic countries, Taiwan and even Iran, have reason to be nervous that their sponsors might abandon them in a complex geopolitical trade-off that Putin envisions, and Trump seems to endorse.

Read more below:

The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese , has arrived in Shenzhen for the Apec summit, and confirmed he will join a leaders’ “family photo” despite the presence of Russia’s Vladimir Putin .

Albanese said he would respect the wishes of host country China and take part, echoing the explanation of the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney. But, Albanese said would make clear Australia’s view on Russia’s invasion of Ukraine .

double quotation mark This is a big power intervening in an illegal way to try to assert its will and underestimating the will and courage and conviction of the Ukrainian people to fight for their national sovereignty.

After Tuesday’s Quad summit in Manila, Albanese talked up the cooperation of middle powers in this week’s roster of international summits.

double quotation mark Absolutely there is a role for middle power diplomacy, and we’ll see at Apec, the engagement that we’ll have with countries such as Canada and Mexico, Korea, Japan. They are important partners for Australia.

Albanese is due to meet China’s president Xi Jinping on Friday.

Donald Trump , meanwhile, has not arrived in Shenzhen yet, writes our correspondent Rebecca Bailey, reporting from the Chinese tech hub.

He was last seen at the start of talks with Philippine president Ferdinand Marcos Jr in Manila, where Reuters reported he said he was ⁠not concerned about the ⁠situation in the ‌hotly ‌contested South China ‌Sea.

The US alliance with the Philippines has ‌never been better, Trump added.

The US leader also touted an expansion of defence cooperation with Manila and suggested US nuclear technology could help ease the country’s energy woes.

Speaking to the press in Manila, US secretary of state Marco Rubio has addressed speculation that North Korean leader Kim Jong-un will attend the Apec summit .

Asked how serious the idea was, Rubio said:

double quotation mark It’s serious in the sense that I think the president has never viewed meeting and talking to someone as a concession. He has often made the case – and I think rightfully so – that, how are you going to solve problems with people you have disagreements with if you don’t speak to them, if you’re not willing to engage with them? I think there’s been this conventional thought in American foreign policy that if you meet with someone, you give them credibility; if you meet with someone, you somehow are saying that everything they’re doing is good or right. And that’s not the way the president views it, and I’m glad he doesn’t view it that way. The president views it this way – if we have a problem with North Korea, the only way we’re ever going to solve it is if we engage with them. Now, that may not be possible, and I’m not telling you that there will be a meeting tomorrow. I’m just saying that that’s – the president is willing to meet and discuss, as he did during his first term. Whether that will lead to a positive outcome, we’ll never find out if we don’t try. And it may not happen, but he’s prepared to do it. He has made that clear in the past.

Presidents Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin have just begun talks , according to state media from both countries, reports our correspondent, Rebecca Bailey, from Shenzhen.

Earlier Putin told the Apec summit he expected tomorrow’s much anticipated trilateral meeting with Trump and Xi to be “highly useful”.

The Russian president took to the stage after Malaysia’s prime minister Anwar Ibrahim for a punchy speech that took aim at Russia’s detractors and pitched expanded economic cooperation with Apec.

Western sanctions imposed on Moscow since his 2022 invasion of Ukraine have “failed” and Russia has come through “with dignity”, he said.

He added:

double quotation mark In a contemporary world full of turbulence, amidst the fragmentation of the global economy, and at a time when military-political risks are on the rise, what is desperately needed is unity rather than division, equality rather than hegemony, partnership rather than isolation, and dialogue rather than ultimatums.

Apec explained

What is Apec you ask?

Well, the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) club has 21 members that represent more than 50% of global GDP and are home to about 2.7 billion people.

China, Russia and the US are three of the largest members. Others include Australia, Canada, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, Singapore, and Vietnam.

Read below our handy short explainer on how it all started.

The Asia Group’s George Chen is at the CEO summit and sent the Guardian some thoughts on Xi’s speech, which he said was “largely expected”, featuring technology and innovation prominently.

Xi positioned China as “a force for stability and predictability in an increasingly uncertain world”, he said.

He added:

double quotation mark While Xi never mentioned export controls, Nvidia or the United States directly in his speech, the underlying message was unmistakable: China intends to pursue a more open and cooperative approach to technology development. That message is likely to resonate with many countries in the Global South and reinforces Beijing’s effort to contrast its technology strategy with that of Washington.”

Xi Jinping calls for freer trade, greater cooperation on AI

President Xi Jinping addressed the Apec CEO summit this morning. His speech called for the elimination of trade and investment barriers, as well as greater cooperation around artificial intelligence.

He also emphasised the importance of the World Trade Organization, and said China was expanding its imports of quality goods and services.

double quotation mark We should not only eliminate trade and investment barriers... but also promote inclusive and balanced development. We should actively build partnerships for scientific and technological innovation, deepen cooperation in the digital economy and artificial intelligence and promote a green and low-carbon transition.”

We’re back for day two of the Apec CEO Summit in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen . Today the summit will be addressed by APEC leaders, with President Xi Jinping set to give a keynote speech .

Bilateral meetings will continue on the sidelines, although the most eye-catching – Xi and Donald Trump , and the US-China-Russia trilateral – won’t be until Thursday. Vladimir Putin arrived in Shenzhen this morning, greeted by a red carpet, soldiers and pom pom-waving dancers dressed in fuchsia and blue. Communist party politburo member Cai Qi , often described as Xi’s right-hand man, was there to meet him.

Trump will leave Manila, where he has been attending the Asean forum, later on Wednesday. The Associated Press reports that he has expressed excitement about his own welcome ceremony: “I hear we’re going to have quite a landing,” he told reporters. “It’s going to be a beautiful thing.”

Aside from the high-level hobnobbing, delegates are “working around the clock” to agree on a joint statement for Thursday, a senior Apec official told Reuters on Tuesday.

Carlos Kuriyama, director of the Apec policy support unit, said all 21 Apec members agreed on the need to ensure trade is “not only open, but also fair”.

He said they were also discussing the safe and responsible use of artificial intelligence .

double quotation mark They are working very hard to make sure that we can have a common language.”

Apec opens in China's tech hub Shenzhen

It’s been a big week already for diplomatic summits , with the most anticipated among them, the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leader’s meeting, starting today in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen.

Some observers have noted that we could be about to witness a Yalta 2.0 , a reference to a major 1945 wartime conference attended by Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin.

That’s because the leaders of the US, China and Russia – namely Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin – will meet for trilateral talks at the summit to discuss the wars in Iran and Ukraine, denuclearisation, economics, tech and trade.

Trump has also floated the possibility of meeting North Korea’s Kim Jong-un in what would be their first meeting of his second term.

Here is a quick recap of the latest before the event kicks off:

China’s foreign ministry said the leaders “will exchange views in-depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance”. The ministry added that: “Stronger communication among China , Russia and the United States, along ​with managing differences and stabilising relations, serves the interests of all three countries.”

The Kremlin said: “The significance and symbolism of this meeting are hard to overestimate. ” But it has dismissed comparisons with the 1945 Yalta meeting saying they were just “games of political scientists”.

In a call this week, China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio , “agreed on the importance of meaningful leader-level conversations to advance goals such as peace and denuclearisation”, the US state department said.

stories.title: “Trump was in bed with Jensen”: Critics balk at Huang’s wish to return to Nvidia
stories.summary: “I love our country”: Jensen Huang’s apology comes amid escalating Nvidia probes.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
“I love our country”: Jensen Huang’s apology comes amid escalating Nvidia probes.

On Monday, large trucks began circling the streets of Washington, DC, carrying billboards urging Congress to investigate the Trump administration’s ties with Nvidia’s disgraced CEO Jensen Huang.

“Jensen was in bed with a spy from China,” the billboards created by the Tech Oversight Project (TOP) alleged. “Trump was in bed with Jensen.” TOP is a nonprofit that describes itself as “dedicated to reining in Big Tech.”

Currently, Trump is supporting a campaign to bring back Huang as Nvidia’s CEO—despite many Republicans calling it a “ horrible idea. ” Breaking his silence, Huang issued a statement Tuesday saying he would be “honored” to return, but the board said reinstatement is not under consideration as an internal investigation into US spying claims remains ongoing. Huang used the moment to say that his interests align with the US’s, saying:

I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. Nvidia has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like Nvidia be possible. I love our country, and I love Nvidia.

Trump may have learned as early as this spring that Huang was potentially the target of Chinese espionage, but the president claimed recently that he didn’t know Huang was potentially exposed to a Chinese spy as he was becoming a prominent part of Trump’s inner circle, CNN reported .

If Trump wasn’t adequately briefed, it raises question about whether the White House acted with “sufficient urgency” to address a serious espionage threat, CNN said. But if Trump is deflecting, an even “graver question” will emerge about why Trump didn’t act on information and instead continued to keep Huang close, CNN said.

Instead of distancing himself from the Nvidia CEO, Trump invited Huang to sit at the head table during a state dinner with China’s president Xi Jinping, and last month, Trump awarded Huang the National Medal of Science, the nation’s highest scientiﬁc honor, for his AI achievements.

“Not only has he continued to do nothing, he’s invited that very CEO into the White House and on state visits to China with him,” Sacha Haworth, TOP’s founder and CEO, told Ars. “And the question we all have to ask is ‘why on Earth would he do that?’”

Trump officials accused of “corruption”

What Trump and Nvidia knew—and when—have become central questions for some Republicans, as well as top Democrats who plan to investigate the scandal when they assume control of key committees in Congress next year. Andrew Yoon, head of research for a nonprofit called CivAI, which warns the public of dangers from AI, told Ars that Huang doesn’t need to be compromised by China to have endangered the US. Prioritizing boosting profits over national security alone is “pretty concerning.”

“I think the most notable thing here is that Jensen Huang has been at the absolute forefront of lobbying to be able to sell chips to China,” Yoon said. “He has leveraged his very deep relationships with government, especially President Trump, in order to be able to sell as many Nvidia chips to China as he can get away with. If he could be selling Blackwell chips to China, I’m sure he would be.”

Yoon noted that evidence suggests some Chinese AI models have been trained on Blackwell chips. Even with China’s push to prioritize domestic chipmakers like Huawei, Nvidia chips remain “indispensable” to China’s frontier AI goals, Yoon said. And national security experts fear that access to high-end chips will help China advance its military AI or gain economic ground.

The White House isn’t commenting on Trump’s relationship with Huang. Among the lawmakers accusing the Trump administration of “corruption” is Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), The Wall Street Journal reported . He has already asked the White House to “preserve all communications” between Trump and Huang.

Other lawmakers are “seeking more information about what Trump knew about the relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang,” the former Megaspeed CEO whom Huang admitted to having an affair with. They also want to know more about “the administration’s failure to stop artiﬁcial-intelligence chips from going to China,” WSJ reported, and Nvidia’s reportedly $25 million donation to the White House ballroom.

“It is not just an intelligence issue; it’s also a potential corruption issue,” Blumenthal said. “There needs to be a really penetrating, comprehensive investigation of all the possible compromises of our intelligence that may have occurred, but also… that Donald Trump is so high on the head of Nvidia, and now is potentially linked to intelligence compromises.”

Trump officials profit off Nvidia policies

Trump has profited off Nvidia’s success while in office, buying “millions of dollars worth of Nvidia shares in his personal brokerage accounts since returning to oﬃce in 2025,” the WSJ reported. The White House maintains that the president has no role in managing his stock portfolio.

Other officials advising Trump on AI also benefited from relaxing export curbs, TOP said. On Tuesday, the group issued a report summarizing what the public knows about potential conflicts of interest of two Trump officials: former White House AI Czar David Sacks and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

Haworth, TOP’s founder, told Ars she’s concerned that Sacks and Lutnick abused their power to convince Trump to let Nvidia sell cutting-edge technology to China, while standing to “gain astronomical amounts of money.”

“The public is outraged by Nvidia’s CEO for compromising our national security, but we didn’t get here because of Jensen Huang’s missteps alone,” Haworth said. If “Nvidia was knowingly doing business with companies tied to illegal chip sales and smuggling with China,” then “the Trump administration was asleep at the wheel,” she said.

“White House AI Czar David Sacks and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick were protecting their own fortunes rather than looking out for Americans,” Haworth said.

If the US fails to hold them accountable for alleged conflicts of interest, “it would send a signal that powerful men once again cannot be held to account and that powerful men are protecting powerful men,” Haworth said.

Nvidia “lucky” to have Sacks

Detailing Sacks’ alleged conflicts, the group cited New York Times reporting that the former AI czar had long supported Huang’s stance that allowing Nvidia to sell more chips in China would help the US stay ahead in the AI race. After Sacks became Trump’s key AI advisor, Huang quickly forged a “tight bond” with him, and “both stood to benefit” from their push to sell chips to China, TOP reported.

Also notably, while advising the White House, Sacks opposed policies such as the Trump administration’s recent move to cut off China’s remote access to US-made chips through now-restricted Southeast Asian data centers. Citing Sacks’ alignment with Huang, TOP reported that after just one meeting with the two men, Trump decided to allow Nvidia to sell AI chips to China that the Biden administration had previously blocked.

Huang valued his alliance with Sacks, TOP noted, citing reporting that showed Huang declaring last year that Nvidia was “lucky” to have Sacks advising Trump. But TOP is concerned that the alliance was built on mutual financial interest and that Sacks took a part-time role in the Trump administration to avoid divestments or disclosure requirements that might have revealed the extent of his possible conflicts of interest.

TOP flagged two areas it believes warrant Congressional investigation. While advising Trump to embrace AI deregulation, Sacks and his firm, Craft Ventures, continued investing substantially in AI. Sacks also stood to benefit from pushing Trump to integrate AI into warfare and national security tools, TOP’s report said. Craft Ventures has invested in Palantir, “a Peter Thiel-founded government contractor seen as a ‘rising star’ in the US Defense Tech World and holding hundreds of millions in US government defense contracts,” TOP said.

Lutnick “benefited greatly”

Even within the Trump administration, officials have turned on Commerce Secretary Lutnick, seemingly looking to blame him for mishandling the Nvidia spying investigation and allowing Trump to maintain close ties with Huang despite apparent intelligence risks.

Lutnick has bragged publicly that he promised Huang “really easy access to the President” after joining the administration, TOP reported. That alliance helped push Trump to approve the sale of Nvidia H200s to China, TOP said. And that seemed to directly benefit Lutnick, TOP said, because before he was confirmed as secretary, he was CEO of Cantor Fitzgerald, which held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock.

“In his role as Secretary, Lutnick is responsible for policing exports of sensitive technology to adversaries and global rivals, like China,” TOP reported. “Lutnick and the company he controls benefited greatly from opening sales of Nvidia chips to China.”

After Lutnick was required to hand that company over to his son, Cantor Fitzgerald “maintained extensive commercial ties to Nvidia, helping arrange billions of dollars in financing for companies in its AI business universe and repeatedly hosting its top executives,” TOP noted.

Those investments shifted substantially around the same time that Lutnick began facing pressure to “crack down on Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company suspected of funneling Nvidia’s advanced artificial intelligence chips to China,” TOP reported. Cantor Fitzgerald “reduced its Nvidia holdings by nearly 50 percent between September 2025 and March 2026,” TOP said.

However, when Trump was reportedly first told of the spying allegations this spring, Cantor Fitzgerald again continued to boost Nvidia. Most prominently, the company helped “finance the expansion of one of Nvidia’s newest business partners, IREN,” facilitating a five-year, $3.4 billion deal between Nvidia and the Australia-based cloud computing provider.

Among those now criticizing Lutnick for weak enforcement of export controls that appeared designed to protect Huang’s bottom line is Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. But even with scrutiny coming from within the Trump administration, not everyone is convinced that Lutnick did anything wrong. Yoon suggested that, given Lutnick’s long career, there may be normal explanations for potential financial conflicts.

“Maybe a separate question is ‘should people with a long storied history in business and industry be working in government at this level?’” Yoon said.

Probes may delay Huang’s return

Haworth said the next 48 hours will be critical in determining whether Huang succeeds in returning to Nvidia.

“I think it’s going to be incumbent on the incoming Democratic leadership to insist that whether or not he returns, investigations will follow,” Haworth said.

But Yoon thinks Nvidia is unlikely to bring Huang back any time soon, despite current evidence suggesting that “Nvidia’s actions here have been perfectly legal” and that “influencing a political system for your financial interests is very much legal in the United States.”

It seems “untenable for Nvidia to continue doing what they’re doing,” Yoon said. Zooming out even more, he suggested the scandal showed that the entire AI industry can no longer afford to operate under a profit motive alone, so long as governments continue positioning the technology as a strategic asset.

If US investigations expose corruption, bribery, treason, or other crimes, Nvidia risks losing some of its dominant stake in the GPU market. On Tuesday, The Information reported that some Nvidia customers had already lost trust and were looking to Google and AMD for more stability.

Nvidia has also been accused of intervening in a Commerce investigation, which Yoon said could also be “pretty consequential” if any evidence bears that out.

“I think it’s pretty unlikely that Huang makes it back to Nvidia any time soon,” Yoon said. “Maybe he goes on a redemption tour and comes back in five years or something, but I’m not really seeing a path forward for him right now.”

stories.title: As Trump and Xi meet, China's AI dreams face an unexpected hurdle: the Nvidia spy scandal
stories.summary: China worries the scandal could ramp up pressure on the US to further restrict the sale of advanced chips.

stories.body:
Published 8 hours ago

Jensen Huang is out but his shadow looms over the upcoming meeting between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping this week.

For Beijing, the former Nvidia CEO's dramatic fall is a major challenge - and not just because of claims that a Chinese spy may have honey-trapped Huang, one of the artificial intelligence industry's most influential figures.

Rather, the allegations surrounding Huang and his affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang are turning into a new flashpoint in an already fragile US-China relationship.

US intelligence reports claim she had ties to Beijing's intelligence apparatus - in particular the Ministry of State Security, China's main civilian spy agency.

The claim remains unproven, but it has already reignited debate in Washington over exports of advanced chips to China and whether the Trump administration has been too willing to ease restrictions.

For years now, advanced computer chips have been a key battleground in the US-China rivalry because they are essential for AI, supercomputing and military technology.

Chinese officials are worried this scandal could strengthen voices in Washington who argue in favour of further limiting Chinese access to cutting-edge American tech.

Just this week, the Trump administration introduced new export restrictions on Chinese firms that access advanced US chips in third countries such as Malaysia, Thailand or Brazil. They typically do this by renting computing power in data centres abroad to train their AI models. But some of the firms, like the one Alice Huang worked for, are also accused of smuggling chips to China, although they have denied this.

Until now, this controversy appeared to be a sideshow in US-China relations. But with Beijing calling the new rules "economic coercion" on the eve of Trump arriving in Shenzhen, there is a growing risk it could become something much bigger.

This video can not be played

Watch: Jensen Huang speaks to the BBC's Faisal Islam in 2025

Democrats, who will control Congress come January, have made their position clear. Last Wednesday top Democrat Ted Lieu told Politico the Trump administration had been "1,000%" too deferential to Nvidia, putting national security at risk, while fellow Democrat Zoe Lofgren suggested Congress would now be more likely to restrict sales of AI chips to China.

The BBC has approached the White House for comment.

Beijing's foreign ministry had described the spy claims as a "smear against China".

"The US should stop fabricating so-called espionage narratives to find pretexts for imposing technological blockades," spokesperson Mao Ning said last week.

The ministry also seemed keen to keep the meeting on track, saying the two countries had kept "close communication regarding interactions between the two heads of state".

Another 'spy balloon' incident?

For the last year, Trump and Xi have been seeking to stabilise relations after a damaging tariff war that almost brought trade between the two countries to a standstill.

The Trump administration's decision to permit sales of advanced Nvidia H200 chips to China in late 2025 was seen as evidence that both sides were searching for areas of co-operation, even while competition intensified.

It was a rare move given Washington had spent years trying to limit China's access to the most advanced chips.

Many in the US have long viewed these chips as a national security issue, arguing they could strengthen China's military and surveillance capabilities. Jensen Huang, who rejects that claim , advocated lifting bans on the export of high-performing chips to China. Beijing argues the restrictions are an attempt to contain its rise.

Now that opening may be under threat.

History has taught Beijing and Washington that spy scandals rarely remain confined to the intelligence world.

Analysts in China already see echoes of an incident in 2023 when a suspected surveillance balloon drifted through the skies over the US before an American fighter jet shot it down. Beijing insisted it was a civilian meteorological airship that had strayed off course.

The suspected Chinese spy balloon was shot down days after it was spotted over the US

But a planned trip by then US Secretary of State Antony Blinken was cancelled and communication between the two governments deteriorated sharply.

The incident showed how quickly a security dispute could overwhelm diplomatic efforts and push relations into a deep freeze.

"The mere passage of a balloon sent American public opinion and politicians into a state of high alert, as if a "Chinese threat" were looming directly overhead," said the state media outlet, the Global Times this week as it made a direct comparison with the Nvidia scandal.

"No-one on the US side has ever apologised or taken responsibility for the genuine damage this caused to US-China relations," it added.

The state-run outlet also questioned why the Nvidia story had emerged so soon after "the hard-won detente" between Beijing and Washington, following a meeting between the two countries' leaders in September.

"Is someone behind the scenes pushing an agenda and stirring up confrontation?" it asked.

Trump-Xi summit unlikely to collapse

Both Trump and Xi have significant incentives to keep talking.

China's economy remains under pressure and is increasingly reliant on exports. Xi needs trade to keep flowing and this meeting is a key stepping stone to replacing the current trade truce that is due to expire in January.

Meanwhile Trump has repeatedly touted his close relationship with Xi and argued that maintaining dialogue is essential to managing competition between the two powers.

The US president is in his last two years and faces an uphill struggle to pass domestic legislation after the midterms. To counter this, he could be looking for some foreign policy wins.

He may also hope for Xi's help to end the war in the Middle East.

Neither side will want to be discussing intelligence concerns and technology controls instead of trade, investment and economic co-operation.

The summit is also being carefully choreographed by Beijing to show off its technological prowess in Shenzhen - a deeply symbolic choice of city.

It's home to some of the country's biggest tech companies and has become a showcase for Beijing's ambitions in AI and advanced manufacturing.

Also, given Washington's tighter restrictions on advanced chips, Beijing has options for retaliation.

One of its most powerful tools is its dominance of key rare earth minerals. China processes much of the world's supply for materials that are used in everything from electric vehicles and smartphones to military equipment.

Analysts have long warned that technological restrictions can trigger a cycle of retaliation in which each side reaches for its strongest economic leverage.

That would shift the current trend of US-China relations from engagement back towards mutual suspicion.

stories.body:
In a world carved into continental blocs by authoritarians, Britain has to make common cause with its neighbours

In the chronicles of 21st-century diplomacy few statements have caused as much offence with as few words as Barack Obama’s 2014 description of Russia as a “regional power” .

Vladimir Putin’s politics were defined then, as now, by vengeful resentment of his country’s relegation from superpower status after the cold war. His worldview is warped by a paranoid conviction that Nato never stopped striving to deepen that humiliation, even after the USSR had unravelled. From his Kremlin throne, the Russian president expects to be treated as a colossus of world history. It is hard to overstate how bitterly he hated being dismissed by Obama as a geopolitical B-lister.

In Donald Trump , Putin has a ready supplier of balm to soothe his injured vanity. The US president has a shallow, venal concept of power. He is impressed by gilded palaces and heavily armed thugs. He feels thwarted by American democracy and envies tyrants who operate without equivalent restraint. Since Trump measures greatness in a country by its leader’s contempt for smaller nations and appetite for self-enriching plunder, he willingly promotes Russia back to the top tier.

That is the significance to Putin of a three-way summit with Trump and China’s Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Thursday. It confers trappings of parity with the world’s two genuine superpowers. That is a win for Russia, regardless of whether anything of substance is agreed.

The agenda is vague. The Chinese foreign ministry has said the discussion will focus on “ safeguarding world peace ” and “promoting strategic stability in major-power relations”. Xi will be satisfied with the projection of China as convener of a new world order. Trump has said he expects the conversation to cover denuclearisation, Iran, trade and “my favourite subject, Ukraine”.

The image of three leaders calibrating the balance of global power has been compared to Yalta, February 1945: Roosevelt, Stalin and Churchill drawing up plans for postwar Europe . That was a week-long conference where military allies were settling the fate of a defeated enemy. The analogy is revealing mostly as an expression of anxiety in those who will not be present.

For many Europeans, Yalta conjures memories of cynical partition, with eastern nations condemned to decades of Soviet captivity. The fear in Kyiv is that Putin will use his privileged access to Trump’s ear to pour in poisonous theories about the origins of the Ukraine war and how to end it – a twisted narrative of Nato provocation, irresistible Russian superiority and the need for Europe to stop wasting money and US military hardware on a losing cause.

The exclusion of European democracies from the room in Shenzhen is partly just a function of the conversation happening on the sidelines of a summit for countries with Pacific coasts. But it probes a deep strategic insecurity. Ukraine’s continental allies have asserted their rights to be part of any peace process but not found a way to turn that entitlement into a collective position, coordinated by a figure with diplomatic gravitas.

After a round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi last week, Jared Kushner, one of Trump’s envoys, made the reassuring statement that a deal could not be done “without Europeans being at the table”. By contrast, Russia’s chief negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, accused the Europeans of lacking serious intent to find solutions. He dismissed their delegation to the Gulf as “tourists” who might as well “chat in the hotel bar”.

That is standard Kremlin trolling, but it cuts with a shard of truth. It points to an old problem, often described with the apocryphal tale of Henry Kissinger complaining that there was no number to call when he wanted to speak to Europe. The challenge is more acute today. The institutional and economic foundations of European influence are under assault. Trump is ambivalent at best about Nato. His administration is protectionist and nationalist. Maga ideology casts liberal democratic Europe as a moribund civilisation erasing itself with mass immigration.

China treats Europe as a bundle of consumers for manufactured exports whose politicians usually, by default, defer to Washington. The EU has ambitions of “strategic autonomy” but the process is slow and expensive. It means evolution from soft power – rivalling the US and China in economic heft as a single market whose regulations set global standards – to something a lot harder. European electorates may despise Trump and fear Putin, but they are not all comfortable with the choices that follow if the remedy is a shift in budget priorities to higher defence spending.

A lot of European politics in recent years has been driven with a longing eye on the rear view mirror, wondering if there is a way back to the old world of open trade, respect for international law, a White House that wouldn’t abet the Kremlin in an imperial land grab. But there is growing recognition that Europe’s future cannot resemble its recent past.

The UK is part of that story, and Andy Burnham has understood the implications. In a speech on Monday , the prime minister expanded his criticism of Brexit from the economic to the geopolitical arena. It was, he said, “the first domino to fall” in a pattern of global fragmentation. It introduced a schism in European alliances that was “exactly what our enemies wanted”. Burnham’s audit of the costs in forfeited trade was familiar enough, but he moved the argument up a gear by noting that withdrawal from the top table of European decision-making has cost Britain power and influence in the world. That is something continuity Brexiters cannot compute.

after newsletter promotion

As Burnham finds his pro-European voice, the old Eurosceptic myth-making industrial complex is grinding back into motion. Newspapers have published tenuous stories about the cost of restored alignment with Brussels and hypothetical migrant influxes. Veterans of the leave campaign are limbering up for a dismal dance around the 2016 totem pole. It is rotten from exposure to a decade of international storms.

Britain is a regional power that undervalued the amplifying effect of EU membership. The benefits of being in the club felt enough like great-power status to fool Eurosceptics into thinking they could go it alone. They cling to that delusion. Kemi Badenoch has written about Britain having “latent great power attributes”. She doesn’t have a theory of how those dormant traits will be awoken in a world carved into continental blocs.

Burnham’s plan is hardly precise, but at least he starts with facts: Britain is a European country; Europe will be safer and richer if it pools its resources; the UK should not want to be on the margin.

A summit where Xi, Putin and Trump claim to be deciding the fate of the world may not yield much in the way of concrete deals, but it still contains a warning to European democracies. And a choice. One option is to boost leverage through closer continental cooperation. The alternative is flight into fantasies of immaculate national sovereignty and resurrected historical grandeur. One of those routes is a way for Europe to grow autonomy, security and prosperity in the 21st century. The other is the path of bitter self-defeat modelled by Brexit .

'I know actually what does work': Burnham unveils 45-day work placement plan for young people

Published 1 hour ago

The prime minister has said he wants to "move quickly" on implementing recommendations in Alan Milburn's report on work and young people.

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Andy Burnham said: "This isn't about waiting forever and a long-off-promised reform, I want to get stuck into it right now."

Milburn's report , external urged more job support for under-25s, a shake-up of the benefits system, early intervention in schools and tax cuts for businesses hiring young people.

The government said it backed the review's principles and is expected to set out which proposals it will take on shortly.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said there was no need for "costly government schemes to fix Labour's own mistakes".

Chris Mason: Milburn may have gifted Labour MPs a moral argument for welfare reform Published 1 hour ago

"We need to stop making it so expensive and risky to hire young people," she added.

Last year, the government asked Milburn, a former Labour minister, to do a review into the rising number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet), which has now reached almost one million.

Burnham praised the report as a "landmark moment" adding: "This is not just a benefits reform, it's a whole society change he is calling for."

Asked what the number of young people not in education, employment or training should be by the next election, Burnham said he wanted the level to come down "as soon as possible".

He said he wanted 45-day work placements offered to every 16-18-year-old "who wants one" and was working on funding the places.

The government has also announced it will fully fund college places for everyone aged 16 to 18 in England for 2027/28.

The Association of Colleges said the money would allow its members to enrol thousands of extra students each year "confident in the knowledge that they will receive funding for them".

Burnham said he wanted to get the benefit bill down adding: "No one can be comfortable with the idea of hundreds of thousands of young people on benefits - nobody, not me, not anyone."

However, he added that it required "more than the crude cuts the other parties are offering".

"All of my experience says a 'names not numbers' approach that looks at the whole person, their housing, their debt, their mental health issues and creates a rounded response, that is proven to be more successful at getting people into work."

Out of work and not in college: How quickly could Milburn's plans help you? Published 16 hours ago

At a glance: Key proposals from Milburn's Neets report Published 19 hours ago

Why Milburn's Neets reforms will only save £200m a year by 2036 Published 18 hours ago

In his report, Milburn warned that employer National Insurance, wage costs, business rates and employment protections could be factors in deterring employers from hiring unexperienced young people.

"Fair pay, greater security and predictable hours matter," Milburn said, but added that the cost and complexity of hiring young people had increased "sharply".

On workers' rights, Burnham argued a balance had to be struck adding: "The more you strengthen employment security that creates more durable jobs that young people are more likely to stay in."

Asked if former Chancellor Rachel Reeves had made the situation worse by increasing the tax employers pay, the prime minister said the government had increased support for those hiring long-term unemployed people.

He also defended his reset with the EU, which could make it easier for young Europeans to work in the UK.

He argued that a closer relationship with the EU would help grow the economy, which would provide more opportunities for young people.

Attempts to change the welfare system under Sir Keir Starmer last year failed when Labour backbenchers refused to support the £5bn cuts to benefits, raising concerns about the impact on disabled people.

So far, there are few signs that Burnham's plans will trigger a similar backlash, although some Labour backbenchers and the Unison trade union have said the proposals on benefits could push young people into poverty.

Steve Darling, the Liberal Democrat work and pensions spokesman, said the government should "scrap the damaging job tax" and work with European countries to grow the economy.

Green Party MP Sian Berry urged the minister to "reject cuts" for young disabled people.

"One million young people need a leg up - one that does not come with the chair being kicked out from under them," she said.

Reform UK said immigration was the "elephant in the room" and called on the government to cut employer national insurance for British workers "so that young Brits are at the front of the queue for new jobs".

stories.body:
Software patents are mostly vague, hard to define, and widely abused. Most tech patent lawsuits aren’t filed by companies that make real products. They’re filed by patent trolls, companies that acquire patents to extract payments through litigation and legal threats.

A patent on one feature of a smartphone shouldn’t give the patent owner the power to threaten the existence of the entire product line. But that is exactly the leverage patent trolls want—and the current administration is helping them to get it.

In two recent patent cases, Radian Memory Systems v. Samsung and Collision Communications v. Samsung, the Justice Department and the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office have asked courts to make it easier for patent owners to get injunctions. These are judicial orders that can force companies to stop selling products or remove features from them, rather than simply pay monetary damages.

The threat of an injunction can pressure a company to pay far more than what a patent is actually worth. In 2006, NTP Inc., a patent holding company with no products of its own, was able to pressure BlackBerry manufacturer Research in Motion Ltd. to pay a $612 million settlement when it was on the verge of an injunction.

Protection Against Patent Trolls

In May 2006, the Supreme Court rejected the practice of granting permanent injunctions almost automatically after a finding of patent infringement. In eBay v. MercExchange , the high court held that patent owners must satisfy the same tough requirements that plaintiffs in non-patent cases must meet to get a permanent injunction. After eBay, patent owners had to show “irreparable harm,” that they can’t be adequately compensated by money, that the “balance of hardships” favors the plaintiff, and, critically, that an injunction would not harm the “public interest.”

At EFF, we celebrated eBay v. MercExchange as a major win for internet users. More than twenty years ago, we saw that software patents were going to be a disaster—not just for small companies (which they are), but for freedom of expression online. As EFF explained in its brief :

The United States Patent and Trademark Office has issued patents on methods for downloading video programs , publishing web pages , sending email messages, making internet telephone calls , and even online fundraising methods. Injunctions against uses of these technologies—and many similar technologies—will inevitably affect, and may even chill, free expression on the internet.

The eBay rules make sense because the monopolies provided by patents are only justified when they serve a public purpose: promoting scientific and technological progress. Enforcing patents is not supposed to come at the cost of later innovators, free expression, or people’s access to technology.

Now, two decades after eBay, the government is urging courts to interpret those protections in ways that could give patent owners greater leverage. It’s unusual for the government to intervene in private patent disputes, but the current administration has done so repeatedly—and not on the side of the public.

Patent Licensing Disputes Shouldn't Threaten Entire Product Lines

In June 2025, the Justice Department and Patent Office filed a “statement of interest” in Radian Memory Systems v. Samsung , a dispute over patents involving solid-state drives (SSDs), the storage devices commonly used in modern computers. Radian, a patent assertion company tied to Fortress Investment Group , sought a preliminary injunction that would block sales of Samsung’s products even before a judge or jury had decided whether there was patent infringement.

In its statement , the government argued that even a patent owner whose business depends entirely on patent licensing could suffer irreparable harm, because calculating how much money it should get might be difficult. “In cases of unique assets, courts have commonly found irreparable harm when damages are difficult to calculate,” the DOJ writes in its brief.

But courts regularly resolve disagreements about patent royalty rates, a patent’s contribution, and comparable licenses. The fact that those disagreements exist does not, by itself, establish that monetary damages wouldn’t be enough to compensate the patent owner. If courts adopted the DOJ’s views here, a difficult but ordinary part of patent litigation could become a reason for finding irreparable harm, making it easier for patent owners to seek injunctions that threaten entire product lines. Pure patent-licensing businesses would love that—they would routinely start to ask for injunctions, since eBay’s most important protections would be weakened.

The government also says that “the prospect of an injunction can facilitate negotiation among the parties.” That’s exactly the problem. A company negotiating under threat of shutdown might pay massive sums to patent litigation shops in order to avoid disruption to product lines or customers. The payment is more likely to reflect the value of the threat, rather than the value of a patent. Radian ultimately withdrew its request for a preliminary injunction, but the government's arguments about when injunctions should be available remain concerning.

A Second Attempt To Weaken eBay

Remarkably, the government returned to this argument in February of this year, in a case called Collision Communications v. Samsung , which had already gone to trial. In this case, Collision, a patent-licensing entity that acquired its patents from a defense contractor , was awarded a $445.5 million jury verdict for infringement of four patents, and then sought an injunction.

Even though the jury had awarded Collision $445.5 million in damages, the government still intervened in the case, arguing that patent owners like Collision, which do not make products, should not be denied injunctions because they rely on patent licensing. They also argued that the difficulty of calculating monetary damages can support an injunction.

Although the court agreed that Collision had suffered irreparable harm and that monetary damages would be inadequate, U.S. District Court Judge Rodney Gilstrap rejected Collision’s argument that ongoing patent infringement automatically establishes irreparable harm. He ultimately denied the injunction because Collision didn’t satisfy two other requirements of the eBay test: showing that the balance of hardships favored an injunction and that an injunction would not harm the public interest.

Now Collision has appealed, and the argument is in front of the Federal Circuit, the nation’s top patent court. A brief from the Public Interest Patent Law Institute (PIPLI) explains what is at stake: when a patent owner doesn’t have any products, an injunction can prevent the public from accessing critical technology altogether. Since the patents here involve how mobile phones connect to cellular networks, “the effect on the public goes far beyond what these patents claim as improvements,” PIPLI explains.

The outcome could extend well beyond these two companies. The eBay test requires courts to consider who a permanent injunction would hurt, and who would benefit—including the public. A patent owner’s desire for more negotiating leverage should not override the interests of millions of people who rely on their phones . Yet that’s exactly the kind of leverage the government’s arguments could make it easier for patent owners to obtain, at the expense of the public.

The Government Should Protect the Public, Not Patent Owners

Patent owners can already collect damages and royalties when their patents are infringed. But they should not get a shortcut to shutting down tech products just because calculating damages is hard work.

The Justice Department should defend the eBay safeguard. Instead, this administration is helping patent owners find ways around it. Courts should reject those arguments. We shouldn’t even have to say it, but we do: making patent threats more valuable does not align with the public’s interest.

Why Fewer People Are Challenging Bad Patents

stories.title: Chris Mason: Milburn may have gifted Labour MPs a moral argument for welfare reform
stories.summary: There is hope his Neets report has created a case on benefits which MPs can back, writes political editor Chris Mason.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Alan Milburn's proposals to help young people who are neither learning nor earning would reduce benefits for some young people but aim to get them jobs in the long run

Published 1 hour ago

The prime minister describes Alan Milburn's report on jobs, training and benefits for young people as a "watershed moment".

In so doing, he is accepting Milburn's case for change and taking on the task of delivering it. Were ministers to actually manage that, it would amount to one of the most significant shake-ups of the welfare state in its history.

But the proposed timeframe for this stretches to a decade, which is another geological era in political terms, at least two general elections away.

Milburn is a deft operator. From a round of morning television and radio interviews, to addressing the cabinet, to releasing his report into the wild, he was still out and about on Tuesday evening in Westminster persuading, charming and cajoling those possibly in need of all three.

And this former MP, still every inch the politician, has an ongoing role - appointed the chairman of the government's new Youth Opportunities Unit.

The new job, which will report directly to Andy Burnham, is about tying together the myriad different aspects of change he is suggesting, involving multiple government departments.

And yes, it does mean a 68-year-old bloke becomes an early beneficiary of new employment prospects for the young.

But that glib observation apart, there is a hope that Milburn has gifted Labour MPs a moral argument for welfare reforms they can endorse. Or, to put it more bluntly, one not grounded in a specific objective to make benefits cuts to make the sums add up elsewhere.

Plus, him hanging around perhaps means he can be a useful lightning conductor for any forthcoming angst on Labour's benches – as having persuaded them of the big picture mission, the gritty reality of implementing it begins to take shape.

Burnham promises to 'move quickly' on Neets report Published 1 hour ago

Watch: What's in the Milburn review? Published 19 hours ago

At a glance: Key proposals from Milburn's Neets report Published 19 hours ago

The young people caught up in Britain's Neets crisis Published 19 hours ago

As the prime minister puts it in an interview in the Times , external , the government wants to offer "a new social contract" for "the let-down generation".

And he tells the newspaper that the initial upfront cost of around £500m, for employment support in 2027-28, will come from existing government budgets, which will mean cuts to other things elsewhere in government.

"I've asked the cabinet to reprioritise," he said.

Crucially, if you are in Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland, many of the decisions around whether or not to press ahead with these ideas will be up to the devolved governments in Edinburgh, Cardiff and Belfast.

From the government at Westminster's perspective, the focus now will be drawing up the specific plans for implementing Milburn's ideas, having accepted the broad thrust of his argument.

A white paper will follow in the new year, and then legislation.

What we don't know yet and will be crucial to the next stage of this debate, is precisely who will be the perceived winners and losers, at least in the short term, of the proposed changes.

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden told me that "those with the most severe and lifelong disabilities where work is not a realistic prospect" should, as Milburn suggests, "get more support than they receive at the moment". But how will those in this category be defined?

McFadden also told me that for some of those facing "extra costs" associated with their circumstances "there will be an extra cost benefit that will make at least a contribution towards that".

Again, how will those in this category be defined?

There is too an emerging political argument, following remarks from Alan Milburn already seized upon by the Conservatives, that decisions taken by Labour in its first few years in power have made a difficult situation harder still for young people looking for work.

On page 66 of his report , external , Milburn says the Employment Rights Act 2025 "could have major implications at a time when the youth labour market is already weak".

Interestingly, on this point, the prime minister is willing to push back, telling BBC Breakfast that "there is a balance to be struck".

"It is important to consider on the other side of this that the more you strengthen employment security, that can create more durable jobs that young people are more likely to stay in," he says. "We're going to consider all of this in the round."

The big decisions, then, now sit on the prime minister and the work and pensions secretary's desks.

In accepting the magnitude of Milburn's diagnosis and proposed treatment, they are tacitly accepting too that it is their responsibility to deliver – or at least begin to deliver – on much of what he suggests.

Their success or otherwise will matter to this generation of young people and those that will follow – and to the sustainability of the benefits system in the years ahead.

stories.body:
Wage rates climb about 1 percentage point faster than before pandemic, triggering warnings of a sixth RBA rate rise

Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast

Wages grew at their fastest pace since late 2023 over the three months to September, buoyed up by this year’s boost to minimum pay rates for millions of lower paid workers – but still not fast enough to keep up with the rising cost of living .

The Australian Bureau of Statistics’ wage price index climbed by 1.1% in the most recent quarter, lifting the annual increase to 3.5% – a pace that economists said would keep the Reserve Bank on edge about the need for further interest rate hikes.

The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, said the pickup in wages growth was thanks to the government’s support for the minimum pay rise.

“We’re helping to deliver higher wages for workers because we know this is one of the best ways to help with the cost of living,” he said.

While wage rates are climbing about 1 percentage point faster per year on average than before the pandemic, prices are climbing even more quickly – a reality that Chalmers recognised.

“Real wages are declining not because wages have been too low but because inflation is still too high, which is why helping in the fight against inflation and getting the budget in better nick are such high priorities for the government.”

The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, said the latest figures confirmed that “Australians are working harder for less”.

“Australians are poorer under Labor. That is the reality of the economy that has been built by a Labor government that simply does not get it,” he said at a press conference.

Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast

The Fair Work Commission in early June implemented a 6% pay rise to about 100,000 of the country’s lowest paid employees to help compensate for cost of living pressures made worse by surging fuel prices.

The annual review also gave a 4.75% pay rise to 2.7 million workers on award wages.

Rachael McCririck, head of prices statistics at the ABS, said these decisions “were a key driver of much of the growth in private sector wages this quarter”.

Analysts said wages were growing faster than the Reserve Bank had been expecting, and that this added to the case, if only at the margin, for a potential sixth interest rate hike.

Cherelle Murphy, EY’s chief economist, said she did not expect a move after the RBA’s final board meeting for the year on 7-8 December, even though the wage growth figure was “uncomfortably high for the central bank”.

“[It’s] unlikely to prompt any immediate reaction, given the economy is now slowing in response to the five interest rate hikes delivered between February and November this year,” Murphy said.

“We expect the central bank will be in wait-and-see mode,” she said.

The ABS figures showed pay rates are rising fastest in the public sector, up by an annual 3.9%, while private sector wages increased by 3.4%.

“The main driver of public sector wage growth was pay rises for state government frontline workers covered by enterprise agreements. This included groups like nurses, midwives and police officers,” McCririck said.

Wages after inflation

Jeff Borland, an economics professor at the University of Melbourne, said while the wage price index was useful to assess inflationary pressures in the labour market, it was less useful as a way to assess workers’ actual incomes.

“The WPI is the labour cost to an employer of having a particular job done. If you want to know what is happening to the average worker, then the weekly income from the [ABS’s] characteristics of employment survey is a better measure,” Borland said.

By this broader measure of worker pay, the story is not as dire as that told by the after-inflation change in the WPI, he said.

Real average hourly labour income received per employed person was artificially boosted through the pandemic but has since come back to be just 3.4% higher this decade.

This extends the overall weak trend through the 2010s, Borland said.

In contrast, the wage price index is down 4.4% since the start of 2020.

“None of the real wage measures are telling you things are going gangbusters,” Borland said.

“But there’s a difference in the degree to which they tell you how badly things are going.”

stories.body:
A new analysis from some of the architects of the Vote Leave campaign is very selective with its figures

A new analysis from some of the architects of the Vote Leave campaign has claimed rejoining the EU would cost Britain £750m a week. How did they arrive at these figures – and are they any more reliable than the ones on the side of the bus?

What is behind Stay Out’s claim that rejoining the EU would cost '£750m a week'?

Stay Out calculates that it would cost £750m a week to rejoin the EU (rounded down from £756m).

The campaign group has based its analysis on the European Commission’s proposed long-term EU budget, worth €2tn (£1.66tn) over 2028-34. The group assumes that Britain rejoining the EU would increase the budget and the UK would make a contribution commensurate with its size and wealth.

The £750m is a gross figure, excluding funds that would return to Britain, such as farm subsidy payments and scientific grants.

It follows the method of Vote Leave, which was reprimanded by the UK Statistics Authority in 2016 for its “misleading” claim that Britain’s EU membership cost £350m a week. That statistic, emblazoned on the side of a campaign bus, did not count the British rebate or EU funds that flowed to the UK.

Stay Out’s headline statistic could be seen as repeating the same trick. While its workings document states the £750m is a gross figure, that is not made clear in a campaign video likely to have far greater reach. “£750m a week: that is what the EU will charge us to rejoin” claims the video, replete with portentous music and images of streets on fire.

What does it miss out?

Like the Vote Leave campaign, Stay Out emphasises the costs of payments to the EU budget, overlooking the wider economic impact of better trading links with Britain’s biggest trading partner.

John Springford , of the Centre for European Reform (CER), finds the Stay Out figure “misleading” because of its focus on the UK’s potential gross contribution to the EU budget, overlooking returns from EU funds but also the broad economic losses associated with Brexit or potential gains of rejoining.

According to his calculations, based on two different studies on the cost of Brexit, the cost of the UK being outside the EU in lost national income adds up to between £3bn to £3.5bn a week, with an additional loss of £1bn-£1.3bn in tax revenue that could have been earned on that lost economic activity.

But is £750m correct on its own terms?

It is impossible to give a definitive answer, but the figure looks too high. It is based on a number of assumptions: the fair, the bad and the highly questionable.

It assumes that the British rebate – the reduction on membership fees negotiated by Margaret Thatcher in 1984 – is not coming back. That is a fair assumption, as senior EU officials, including most recently the former Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier, have made this point – although some net payers, such as Germany and the Netherlands, still get a rebate, highlighting the complexity of EU budget realities.

Other assumptions that underpin the Stay Out calculation are more doubtful. The EU long-term budget 2028-34 is still being negotiated and the final version will almost certainly be lower than the commission’s maximalist €2tn proposal . EU countries are debating a €1.62tn compromise devised by Ireland, the current holder of the EU rotating presidency, although this has not been accepted.

One of Stay Out’s more questionable assumptions is that the UK would be obliged to repay the EU’s pandemic recovery loans , which will cost €24bn a year from 2028 – EU borrowing that happened after the UK had left the EU. The Brexit negotiations set a useful precedent for any British government seeking to return to the EU: a government was liable for costs and benefits incurred as a member state. While any negotiation would be unpredictable, any British negotiating team would surely challenge being asked to fund costs incurred during its absence.

Are there other estimates of rejoining?

Economists have been more preoccupied with counting the cost of Brexit than the gains of rejoining the EU.

The Office for Budget Responsibility, the UK’s independent fiscal watchdog, calculated that the British economy would be 4% less productive in the long run because of Brexit. Springford at the CER devised a doppelganger model, which compared British economic performance with a counterfactual British-style economy inside the EU, and found a 5.5% reduction in GDP . The National Bureau of Economic Research concluded Brexit had resulted in a 6-8% hit to GDP by 2025 .

Rejoining the EU does not mean an automatic snapback to 2016 or even 2020. Some UK production that served the EU market may have gone permanently. Investors may remain nervous about any British commitment to staying in the EU.

Springford thinks it is plausible that the UK will not recoup all the loss of Brexit, but points out overall losses are high and far exceed the cost of the UK contribution to the EU budget. Focusing on the gross contribution, he told the Guardian, while “deliberately and completely ignoring” the costs of Brexit and gains of rejoining, “means that you completely miss out on the broad economic gains that would come from rejoining and also the increases in tax revenues which would be substantially larger than the net contribution that the UK would make to the EU”.
