stories.title: How new US chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China
stories.summary: The new rules restrict chip exports and also access to their computing power, which China relies on heavily.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Xi and Trump when they met in Beijing in May

Published 17 November 2026

As US President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors.

On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.

The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models.

South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market.

But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China.

This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. At least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027, according to research by the Institute for Progress , external , a US-based think-tank.

China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing "will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests".

A blow to Asia's AI boom

This is also a problem for South East Asian economies where large numbers of data centres have sprung up recently. Some of the firms behind them are accused of helping China evade US export controls on advanced chips.

One of those is Singaporean data centre firm Megaspeed, whose former director Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese spy. Calls for tighter export controls have grown after Nvidia's Jensen Huang admited to an affair with her and resigned as CEO .

Megaspeed, the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia, is accused of illegally smuggling chips to Chinese companies after purchasing them for use in data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

The company has denied these allegations, defended its business as "legitimate and lawful", and said it has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". It also said Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director in late 2023 and left the firm last year.

The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, however, has said Brazil and the four South East Asian nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" of the chips that Washington wants to keep out of China's hands.

The new measures are aimed at ensuring sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the bureau added. Licences will be issued on a "case-by-case basis", it said.

Batam in Indonesia is emerging as a major regional data centre hub

Countries like Malaysia and Thailand whose data centre roll out has been heavily driven by Chinese buyers could be hit hardest, says international trade expert Naoise McDonagh from Australia's Edith Cowan University.

But the new rules are unlikely to derail the data centre boom as a whole, says Reema Bhattacharya from advisory firm Verisk Maplecroft, adding that investment backed by major tech firms and clearly identifiable customers should "remain relatively resilient".

Singapore was an early adopter of data centres but when it began limiting new construction, investment flowed to neighbours Malaysia and Thailand. Johor in Malaysia and Batam in Indonesia have also approved billions of dollars worth of data centres to catch the spillover demand.

These countries have been offering incentives such as cheaper land to attract foreign investment, including from Chinese tech giants Alibaba and Tencent.

But now, the region could find it harder to get hold of advanced chips.

The BBC has contacted Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand for comment.

Singapore said it is "engaging relevant US authorities" to understand the new rules better, and is "exploring how to facilitate trusted access" for local firms.

A spokesperson for Brazil's Ministry of Development, Industry, Trade and Services said it is aware of the US announcement and it "is closely monitoring any potential developments regarding this measure".

Malaysia previously said it welcomes data centre investment but "will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls".

A headache for China

The new rules also come just ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week.

Beijing has made self-sufficiency in tech a national priority and needs the best chips to build powerful AI models.

Chinese firms DeepSeek and MoonShot have come close to US rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI. So much so that The Institute for Progress estimates top US AI models lead the best Chinese platforms by only about six and half months.

"This is despite US AI companies having significantly better compute access and financing," it said.

Still, China needs advanced US chips to ensure its best AI models are competitive, experts tell the BBC.

The new restrictions on South East Asia and Brazil have taken away "one of the more practical routes Chinese AI developers had to accessing frontier computing power," Bhattacharya said.

But tighter restrictions could also push Chinese firms towards domestic semiconductors and further drive advancement at home.

That has been a longstanding dilemma for Washington, McDonagh said: whether to keep selling chips to China to retain its reliance on the US, or restrict access and risk further spurring Chinese innovation.

stories.summary: Darren Jones MP, the former chief secretary to the prime minister under Keir Starmer, recently called for a new multinational treaty governing the safe development and use of superintelligence (where AI substantially surpasses humans across most cognitive tasks). He also argued that Britain’s growing reputation for AI safety and trustworthiness made it a good conduit for such collaboration. What I found most interesting about this intervention was not the question of whether AI could pose a threat to humanity. Instead, it was a management and organisational question sitting underneath it: “can our systems of governance keep pace with the development of AI intelligence while also ensuring it is safe?” We are at a moment in history where global tech leaders and some of their employees believe there is a greater than 10% chance that AI could kill all humans within the next decade. But humans are still struggling to understand the potential consequences of AI; by the time we do it may be too late to act. He also argued that Britain’s growing reputation for AI safety and trustworthiness made it a good conduit for such collaboration.

What I found most interesting about this intervention was not the question of whether AI could pose a threat to humanity. Instead, it was a management and organisational question sitting underneath it: “can our systems of governance keep pace with the development of AI intelligence while also ensuring it is safe?”

We are at a moment in history where global tech leaders and some of their employees believe there is a greater than 10% chance that AI could kill all humans within the next decade. But humans are still struggling to understand the potential consequences of AI; by the time we do it may be too late to act.

However, we must be careful to distinguish this prediction from the current risks and what might happen as AI systems become able to independently improve themselves (full recursive self-improvement ) and move towards superintelligence .

I concur with calls for a multinational treaty and for the UK to take a leading role. As a business scholar, I also believe research from some business schools can inform us about managing and organising systems whose complexity, speed and autonomy are increasing faster than our capacity to understand them.

This is familiar territory in high hazard industries such as nuclear energy and aviation. Here, two theories are particularly relevant: normal accident theory , associated with the US sociologist Charles Perrow, and high reliability theory , associated with the work of American political scientist Todd LaPorte. Taken together, they could provide a powerful framework for thinking about AI safety and regulation.

‘Normal’ accidents

Normal accident theory begins with an uncomfortable proposition. In complex, interdependent systems, such as nuclear power plants or spacecraft built to carry humans, accidents are not necessarily the consequence of individual incompetence, negligence or bad design. They can emerge from the interaction of multiple components in ways that are difficult to anticipate.

In such systems, events happen rapidly. When something unexpected takes place, there may be little time to intervene between one potential failure and the next. This can lead to a cascading error, with the potential to cause a catastrophe. An often-used example is the partial meltdown at the Three Mile Island nuclear plant in Pennsylvania, US, in 1978. The accident occurred because of a combination of mechanical malfunction, instrument faults and human factors.

The risks further increase when you add AI agents into such a complex system – AI agents are systems that carry out tasks in response to instructions. Examples might include financial systems, software development systems, scientific databases in labs or even systems that connect lots of agents.

In any such system, an individual component – including the AI agent – might meet acceptable quality thresholds; the difficulty lies in the interactions between them and our understanding of these interactions. Part of the problem is that we know agents’ behaviour can be unpredictable: recent reports have described AI agents behaving in ways that their developers did not expect .

The UK government has highlighted risks associated with increasingly capable AI agents and has stressed the importance of testing frontier AI models and developing a scientific understanding of their capabilities.

If AI systems become more autonomous, more interconnected and faster moving, the conventional idea of a “human in the loop”, to correct major errors, could become increasingly challenging.

No fate but what we make?

High reliability theory offers a counterpoint. The high reliability tradition emerged from research into organisations that were operating technologies where failure could have catastrophic consequences, such as nuclear power plants, aircraft carriers and air traffic control.

Its central insight is almost the opposite of a pessimistic reading of normal accident theory. Essentially, it says that organisations can develop practices and cultures that allow them to operate extraordinarily complex technologies with very low failure rates . In fact, we have seen this with the electricity system, space travel and bioengineering.

These organisations achieve high reliability because their baseline assumption is that they are not safe . They remain attentive to hints of bigger problems, do not automatically dismiss anomalies, learn from near misses and failures and build redundancy – for example, backing up offline systems and providing kill switches.

They routinely rehearse failure, establish operational processes, adhere to regulation for safety and assurance, comply with professional standards and certification schemes and have independent oversight. High reliability organisations give experts the authority to challenge decisions. They continuously learn from their performance.

This provides a very different way of thinking about AI governance. Instead of asking simply, “how do we regulate AI?” we should ask: “what would a high-reliability organisation look like if AI was embedded throughout it?”

This suggests that AI safety cannot be reduced to a model passing a one-off technical test before deployment. It must span different organisations and transcend international boundaries.

AI assurance

This is where the current political conversation about AI regulation risks being too narrow. Governments need to understand what frontier laboratories are developing. But government cannot realistically sit permanently inside every AI company and inspect every model.

Nor can legislation anticipate every technical configuration that AI will take. The UK government recognises it must cultivate trustworthiness in AI through assurance. Assurance asks whether there is credible evidence that a system is behaving within defined boundaries, whether those boundaries are appropriate, whether risks are being monitored and whether someone is accountable when they are breached.

The aircraft industry has engineering standards, certification regimes, professional qualifications, independent inspection, incident reporting and regulatory oversight.

Nuclear power operates within an elaborate ecosystem of safety engineering and regulatory assurance. Financial institutions and medicine both have sophisticated systems of assurance.

AI is becoming increasingly consequential, yet its assurance infrastructure remains comparatively immature. This is particularly striking given the speed at which frontier systems are developing. The institutional challenge is not simply to produce more AI regulation, but to create the professional safety culture that makes regulation meaningful.

A potential new multinational treaty on the safe and regulated development of superintelligence would frame AI safety as a rapidly evolving global challenge. At the same time, it potentially creates a once-in-a-generation opportunity for the UK to help shape the emerging architecture of AI governance.

stories.body:
Former Labour minister Alan Milburn has finally delivered his long-awaited report on the UK’s nearly 1 million young people who are not in education, employment or training ( Neet ). In it, he proposes guaranteed work or training opportunities for all 16 to 24-year-olds, but also outlines the need to shift the focus away from benefits. It will be up to the government to decide which ideas to take forward, but our panel of experts has assessed some of the key issues.

Changed landscape for Labour on welfare reform

Tony McNulty, teaching fellow and lecturer in British politics and public policy

Everything about the ongoing debate by government around the issue of welfare reform is different this time. Former prime minister Keir Starmer’s attempts to secure reform in July 2025 could not have been organised in a worse fashion. Talk of it being a “confidence issue” was always a nonsense, real or imagined.

The rebellion happened in the context of severe restrictions on the winter fuel payment , the government’s insistence that it was not going to scrap the two-child benefit limit and its own assessment that the benefit moves would push an estimated 250,000 people into poverty. Within months of the Labour government being elected, it looked as though it had forgotten the reason for its very existence.

Whatever the intention, these plans were seen to be bereft of any sense of Labour values. This time around, the world has changed. Crucially, the three key architects of the rejected policy (Starmer, his chancellor Rachel Reeves and his work and pensions secretary Liz Kendall) have all gone – banished to the back benches or off to find pastures new.

The winter fuel payment was revisited and this allowance is now means-tested . The two-child benefits limit has been scrapped. An anti-poverty strategy has been articulated. Labour now has in Andy Burnham what many of the former rebels will see as a Labour PM.

Crucially, the ground has been prepared and the pitch has been rolled – by the whips office, the cabinet and by Burnham. It now feels like the debate is on Labour terms, unlike last summer. It is no accident that there has been an ongoing, sometimes subterranean, debate focusing on what to do with nearly a million young people on benefits who could and perhaps should work.

Milburn’s focus has been on this young cohort first and foremost – and couched in terms of working with them to ensure a productive role and meeting their expectations and aspirations. A Labour debate in Labour language. A political strategy and a government that takes its backbenchers seriously. This is miles from where it was last year. Although success is not guaranteed, the government now has a fighting chance to secure reform on its own terms – and that matters.

New guarantees must be appropriate

Lisa Russell, professor of education and employment

Young people do not suddenly become Neet at 16. While Alan Milburn’s focus on opportunities rather than long-term benefit dependency is to be welcomed, work that my colleagues and I have done on Neets suggests this is something of a blunt instrument for such a complex picture.

Our findings suggest that simply guaranteeing young people work or a placement ignores any long-terms effects that they might experience as a result of years of living with unmet needs. These could include poor mental health, bullying, disrupted education or undiagnosed and unsupported special educational needs and disabilities (Send).

Read more: We know which young people are most likely to end up Neet in England – but not why

Our five-year study, Mapping interventions for Neet young people in England , shows that the quality of support matters. Milburn’s proposal guarantees eligible young people a fully funded, six-month job. But there is an important difference between providing meaningful opportunities and requiring young people to participate in something that does not meet their needs. If education, training or employment pathways are poorly matched to a young person’s circumstances, the risk is that they’re left feeling frustrated and disengaged. This will not improve outcomes for anyone.

The report includes proposals for a “youth allowance” to replace personal independence payments (Pip) for under-25s and the health element of universal credit. But lasting change requires more than welfare reform alone. Alongside employment support, there needs to be less rigidity and less focus on exam outcomes in secondary schools. There’s also a wider need for better mental health provision and stronger support for young people whose needs have too often gone unrecognised. An “opportunity guarantee” can only work if the opportunities themselves are genuinely inclusive and supportive.

Previous policy hasn’t helped young workers

Rachel Scarfe, lecturer in economics

There are many costs to employing a worker, beyond the headline hourly or annual wage. The increase in employers’ national insurance contributions last year for workers aged 21 or over was just one in a series of these rises. There were also increases in 2019 to the automatic enrolment pension contributions that employers have to make, and sick pay was improved in 2016 as part of the Employment Rights Act. These costs are all linked to wages, so when wages increase, the cost of national insurance, pensions and benefits such as sick pay increase as well.

This is exactly what happened when Labour lowered the age limit for the national living wage from 25 to 21 in 2024. Employers often attempt to pass on their extra costs to workers by paying them lower wages. If this isn’t possible (because of a rising minimum wage), they may instead reduce hiring. In some cases, they may choose not to employ a young worker at all.

By proposing to abolish employers’ national insurance contributions for workers aged under 25, and recommending that automatic pension enrolment should not be expanded further, Alan Milburn has recognised this issue. The proposed cut in national insurance contributions is targeted at employers in retail and hospitality. These sectors employ many young people, often on the minimum wage. As a result, the joint effects of a rising minimum wage and increases in other costs are greater than in other sectors. Young people’s job prospects may have suffered as a result.

Employers should resist AI

Fabian Stephany, lecturer in AI and work

There is an economic reason to believe that AI is negatively affecting the entry-level jobs that young people typically apply for. Ultimately, a fundamental change is required. Both young and old people should be advised to have a basic understanding of AI and integrating it into their workplace. Much like with the introduction of computers decades ago, it’s fair to expect that everybody will be required to work with AI to some extent.

However, many entry-level positions are defined by repetitive, standardised work – or commodity work – for example, writing emails and memos or preparing presentation slides. AI does these tasks easily, making it a short-term economic incentive for companies to replace their junior workers with AI, and contributing to the Neet issue. Similarly, with “AI-washing” , companies can let go of junior employees while using AI as a scapegoat.

However, from my point of view, the problem is much more far-reaching. Companies are cutting off their own talent pipeline by not investing in junior workers, as they will not have experts five or ten years down the road. This will have dramatic consequences, as experts are needed more, not less, when it comes to AI. Firms would see long-term gain if they invested in developing young people’s skills.

To escape this dilemma, the government should do everything it can to incentivise firms to focus on the human. Though it can cost employers when young people make mistakes while they’re learning, companies should instead speed up the process of building staff expertise in using AI.

stories.title: They Suffered Brain Injuries After Riding a Six Flags Roller Coaster. Regulators Pinned the Blame on Them.
stories.summary: The post They Suffered Brain Injuries After Riding a Six Flags Roller Coaster. Regulators Pinned the Blame on Them. appeared first on ProPublica .

stories.body:
Co-published with L.A. Material

Reporting Highlights

Scant Scrutiny: After people died or were hospitalized soon after riding Six Flags’ X2 roller coaster, California regulators often did minimal or no inspection.

Riders’ Responsibility: California regulators have regularly accepted Six Flags’ assertions that riders’ injuries could not be the fault of the X2.

Insufficient Inspectors : A 2025 audit found that the state agency enforcing roller coaster safety had been short-staffed for years.

These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.

A 17-year-old boy died after riding the extreme X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in California this summer, just weeks before two more people suffered severe brain injuries after riding the same attraction, ProPublica and L.A. Material have found.

A homicide detective investigating Christopher Gibson’s death in June sent an email to the California official responsible for ensuring roller coaster safety. But records show that the official did not reply until nearly two months later. The lack of action raises the question of whether the brain damage suffered by the two riders the following month could have been avoided.

Christopher’s death, which has not been previously reported, also raises questions about Six Flags, its flagship X2 ride and the way in which California regulates roller coasters.

Billed as a “fourth-dimension” roller coaster, the X2 drew more than 16 million riders attracted to extreme thrills. It featured seats that swiveled in all directions as the ride hurtled and twisted along the track, sometimes at a rate of up to 76 mph.

The X2 was shut down temporarily after two separate brain hemorrhages in July. In August, CNN reported that the X2 had been “linked to more than a dozen reports of serious injuries” and two deaths over nearly two decades.

Christopher’s is a third.

A ProPublica and L.A. Material investigation has found that state regulators have repeatedly failed to take swift action in the face of reported deaths and head injuries on the X2. On at least 70 occasions since 2010, Magic Mountain reported head injuries to the little-known unit within the California Division of Occupational Safety and Health responsible for ensuring roller coaster safety.

But rather than responding to those reports with vigorous inspections or safety checks, the regulators often did minimal or no investigation, according to a ProPublica and L.A. Material analysis of court filings, public records and internal regulatory documents.

“How many more people have to die before you think, ‘Well, maybe we should look at that?’” said Mariusz Ziejewski, a biomechanical engineer who has worked with the military to reduce brain injuries and was an expert witness in a lawsuit against Magic Mountain. “I think one is already way too much.”

CalOSHA and Magic Mountain instead frequently blamed riders for their injuries and in more than 35 cases alleged that people had somehow ridden the attraction incorrectly by failing to hold their heads in the right position. In one case, when a 14-year-old was hospitalized last year after losing consciousness on the ride, officials attributed it to the teenager’s menstrual cycle.

Six Flags and CalOSHA did not respond to detailed questions from ProPublica and L.A. Material. However, Denisse Gómez, a spokesperson for the state department that oversees CalOSHA, said in a statement that when theme park injuries are reported, regulators evaluate whether the ride was operating correctly and according to state safety rules. The agency is “committed to public safety,” she said, adding that “because that investigation is ongoing, we are not commenting on matters involving X2 at this time.”

Six Flags provided a statement that noted that the X2 had consistently passed safety tests, and its parks undergo preventative maintenance and a comprehensive, third-party inspection program. They also said their investigation of the ride remains ongoing, and that they are fully cooperating with CalOSHA. “Safety is our ethos and is at the heart of everything we do,” a spokesperson said.

When Six Flags has been sued for wrongful death or injuries related to the X2, it has maintained that injuries are rare and the ride is highly regulated by CalOSHA. In a recently settled lawsuit related to 22-year-old Christopher Hawley, who died after riding the X2 in 2022, Magic Mountain’s director of public safety said in a declaration that the state has never notified the park of any “patron safety-related concerns related to the acceleration forces on the X2.”

Christopher Gibson was an autistic but healthy teen when he and his mother, Leanndra Fascaldo, drove from their Colorado home to California to celebrate his high school graduation at Magic Mountain.

The pair rode roller coasters for several days starting on May 31, including the X2 and the Viper, which Christopher called a “neck breaker,” according to a sheriff’s report. On their fourth day at the theme park, the teen once again rode the X2 and then the Great American Revolution before complaining of a headache. By early afternoon, they returned to the hotel.

That night, the pain grew worse. His mother gave him Advil. Eventually, he moved to the hotel room’s closet, where it was darker, and went back to sleep. His mother assumed he was just exhausted, but around 2 p.m. the next day she noticed that he had stopped snoring. She looked into the closet and saw that his lips were blue and his face was covered with “white and pink foam.” She called 911. Paramedics pronounced him dead at 3:16 p.m. on June 4.

Within a month, a sheriff’s homicide detective reached out to the California state office that regulates roller coasters, writing that “it is possible that he suffered an injury during his visits to the theme park.” The detective did not receive a reply until she contacted the office again two months later.

It’s been a deadly year for Six Flags. In addition to the California incident, an Atlanta school worker died in October after riding one of the theme park’s “hypercoasters” at Six Flags Over Georgia, prompting the company to temporarily close nine attractions at six theme parks across North America.

Theme park rides are regulated by states, not the federal government. In 2000, the legislature gave CalOSHA, the agency responsible for worker safety in California, oversight of roller coasters. Millions of people flock to the state’s theme parks each year, and the move came after a series of high-profile accidents in the 1990s. Under the law, state officials were given new power to conduct annual inspections , and theme parks must report accidents that result in serious injury to the agency.

But ProPublica and L.A. Material found that officials in CalOSHA’s Amusement Ride and Tramway Unit have frequently determined that investigations are unnecessary when accidents happen on the X2.

In 16 instances involving people who wound up in the hospital after riding the X2 between 2009 and 2022, CalOSHA invoked identical or similar language after checking a box on accident reports that said state action was not called for. “At this time, this accident does not warrant an investigation,” said one typical form. “The condition which developed while the patron was riding does not appear to be related to the maintenance or operation of the ride.” The report was filed in response to a woman who was hospitalized in 2016 with a head injury after riding the X2.

This also held true in cases where people lost their lives. When Hilda Farias suffered a massive brain hemorrhage after riding the X2 in October 2010, CalOSHA officials adopted similar language and conducted no inspection. The state regulator’s report did not even note that the 28-year-old mother of a 5-year-old had died, according to records obtained by ProPublica and L.A. Material. Farias’ family sued the theme park, and the case settled in 2015.

When Hawley died in June 2022 after riding the X2, Magic Mountain initially told CalOSHA that the cause appeared to be heatstroke, according to a state report. The coroner later determined that Hawley, like Farias, had died of a massive brain hemorrhage. On that occasion, CalOSHA shut the ride down briefly while Six Flags conducted tests to measure the impact of g-forces on the rider and examined maintenance records. It ultimately determined that the ride was operating normally, according to a CalOSHA inspection obtained by ProPublica and L.A. Material.

Christopher Gibson wore a Batman hoodie to school almost every day.

Diagnosed with autism when he was 5 or 6, Christopher was “high-functioning and verbal,” his mother told a sheriff’s detective. He had recently graduated high school and was headed to Colorado Mesa University to study theater.

As part of a family tradition, the teen’s mother let each of her five children pick the location of a celebratory senior trip. Chistopher wanted to ride roller coasters, and mother and son discussed a trip to Disneyland or Disney World. After some online research, Christopher chose Six Flags Magic Mountain, known for its thrill rides and DC Comics characters.

“He wanted to see Six Flags,” said Chadwick McGrady, an attorney representing the family in Christopher’s death. “The marketing worked.”

Magic Mountain sits about 35 miles north of downtown Los Angeles, in Valencia, the last notable stop before Interstate 5 climbs a steep stretch known as the Grapevine and drops down into the San Joaquin Valley. The park is aptly named: Roller coasters built into the mountainous terrain hurtle riders down hillsides and through trees, with disorienting turns taken at high velocity.

Christopher rode the X2 on June 2 and again on the morning of June 3. Soon after, reeling from a headache, he texted his mother from a park restroom: “I don’t think I can do any more today. My head is hurting me.”

They went back to the hotel. He had two days to recover before one of the big draws of the trip: DC Heroes and Villains Fest. Christopher “was a huge fan of DC Comics and was looking forward to meeting Batman on Friday, when DC Comics characters would be at the park,” sheriff’s detective Yoon Nam would later write in her report. Friday, June 5, was its opening day, and Christopher was determined not to miss it.

But on the morning of June 4, his head was still hurting him. He had taken refuge in the hotel room’s closet. His mother wasn’t unduly alarmed, because Christopher often retreated to dark spaces at home, a longstanding self-soothing ritual. She listened to the sound of his snoring — until at some point in the afternoon, the sound stopped.

In a statement released through her lawyer, Fascaldo said that her son “had so many dreams, and had his whole life ahead of him.”

After an autopsy, the County of Los Angeles Medical Examiner found a large subdural hemorrhage. The cause of death: “blunt force head trauma.” The reason for the injuries was noted as a “history of theme park rides.”

Nam and the medical examiner spoke by phone with Fascaldo, Christopher’s mother, on June 6.

According to a source familiar with the investigation, Fascaldo was composed, recounting a precise chronology of the rides Christopher had ridden. Among them were Full Throttle and the Viper, and, at least twice, the X2.

Nam contacted CalOSHA. She knew that it was responsible for regulating the state’s roller coasters and wanted to make sure the agency was aware that the Magic Mountain rides could have contributed to Christopher’s death.

“I cannot attribute his death to his roller coaster ride experiences with 100% certainty,” Nam wrote in a July 2 email to Bobby Park, who runs the CalOSHA unit regulating roller coasters. “However, at this time, it is possible that he suffered an injury during his visits to the theme park.”

The detective offered to help. “Please let me know if this case warrants additional follow-up by your office,” she wrote. “Feel free to call, text, or email with any questions or concerns.”

In the days after that unanswered email, more parkgoers suffered injuries after riding the X2.

On the evening of July 5, three days after the homicide detective sent her email, Pamela Guillen, 39, rode the coaster with her daughter.

When the car she was riding in trundled back into the station, Guillen’s daughter saw that her mother was “sitting with a vacant stare and her mouth open,” according to a lawsuit the family recently filed. Six Flags has not yet filed a response.

Guillen, who was visiting from Hawaii, managed to stumble off the ride, but a few minutes later park EMTs found her lying unconscious at the exit ramp. Two hours later, Gary Newman, the park’s vice president of maintenance, phoned CalOSHA to report the accident, relaying that a relative had said: “My cousin seemed out of it when she got off the ride so we took her to a bench and she went unconscious.”

The next morning, Scott Prather, a senior safety engineer with CalOSHA’s theme park unit, emailed his boss. According to a state official who has viewed the email, Guillen had been diagnosed with a brain bleed and was going into surgery. The email also said that the ride had been closed for inspection and g-force testing to ensure it was operating as intended.

Six Flags hired a firm that specialized in amusement park rides to conduct the test, according to a CalOSHA source familiar with the investigation.

State officials reviewed the results and authorized Magic Mountain to reopen the ride, the source said.

Then, on July 9, there was another incident, according to CalOSHA records reviewed by ProPublica and L.A. Material. A woman from Nevada was visiting Magic Mountain with her family and others. They were roller coaster enthusiasts and had saved the X2 for their last ride of the day.

As soon as the ride started, the woman sensed something was wrong, according to an email she later sent to CalOSHA’s general inbox.

“The back of my head was repeatedly and forcefully slammed against the back of the seat,” she wrote in the email, which was reviewed by ProPublica and L.A. Material. “I tried holding my head forward and tried pushing it back against the seat to stop the banging, neither worked.”

When the ride stopped, she wasn’t sure whether she could stand. She couldn’t turn her head from side to side. She had nausea, sensitivity to light and a headache that reached “approximately 9 out of 10.”

She wasn’t the only one. “Three of the eight people riding together experienced similar difficulty with their heads repeatedly striking the backs of their seats,” she wrote in August.

She also filed a formal complaint with Six Flags in July but has not received a response, she told ProPublica and L.A. Material.

Two days after the Nevada woman rode the X2, there was another, more serious injury.

Naomi Greer-Wilkinson, a healthy 25-year-old from Los Angeles, rode the X2 on the night of July 11.

According to a lawsuit her family filed in September against the park, Greer-Wilkinson came off the ride “confused and having difficulty walking.” She stumbled off and then lost consciousness. She has since had multiple emergency brain surgeries. The lawsuit says she “remains bedridden, ventilator dependent, unable to speak.” Six Flags has not responded to the lawsuit.

On July 12, the X2 was temporarily shut down. It has not reopened.

In the wake of the ride’s closure, many amusement park patrons are asking how regulators could have missed so many signs of danger.

California law requires CalOSHA to audit records related to every permanent ride each year, including reports of accidents. When amusement park patrons are seriously injured on rides, the theme park must notify regulators immediately .

And yet, again and again, records show, regulators accepted Six Flags’ assertions that the injuries people suffered were not the fault of the X2. ProPublica and L.A. Material reviewed the state’s reports on X2 riders who were taken to the hospital from 2009 to 2022. In more than two-thirds of the cases, or 17 out 23, CalOSHA checked “no” on the form that would determine whether an investigation was warranted.

In September 2022, less than three months after Hawley died, a 28-year-old woman passed out as she exited the ride and hit her head, according to Magic Mountain’s account of the accident in a report filed with the state Paramedics took her to Henry Mayo Newhall Hospital.

Two days after the woman’s injury, Park determined no investigation was necessary. Park wrote: “Patron has pre-existing TBI [traumatic brain injury], diabetes, and has not eaten or consumed anything throughout the day.”

The woman, who survived the incident, sued Six Flags, which denied fault. The case settled in 2025.

The pattern of regulators citing preexisting conditions or rider behavior went back years. In 2011, the state noted that a 21-year-old woman had “a history of panic attacks,” so no investigation of the ride was necessary after she complained of a head injury.

In 2016, a 49-year-old woman hit her head against the headrest and asked for an ambulance. CalOSHA noted that her condition “does not appear to be related to the maintenance or operation of the ride,” adding that she “did not keep her head back” as riders are instructed.

Park declined to comment.

Some of the failures appear related to staffing shortages at CalOSHA. According to a 2025 staffing study by a Sacramento consulting firm commissioned by the state, audits of amusement park rides can be brief. The annual audit for a ride in X2’s class — a review meant to cover accident reports, training and maintenance reports and inspections — lasted an average of 3.7 hours.

The study also found that CalOSHA’s ride unit had been short-staffed for at least three years, with vacancies for its top job and two of four supervisor posts. There were “insufficient” supervisors for “thorough field supervision” and “inspection report review,” the report found.

Documents obtained by ProPublica and L.A. Material show Park had voiced frustration about staffing for his division since at least 2019. In an email he sent last week to his supervisor and the state department that oversees CalOSHA, Park wrote: “We have done workload studies, classification studies, begged, pleaded, and warned of the impending doom, and we are still no further along than we were 11 years ago.”

He continued: “We have failed. I have tried to do this, but I cannot continue as the dwindling supply of tools has run out.”

Park had been the CalOSHA official who received the news of Christopher Gibson’s death from Nam, the homicide detective, in early July.

In late August, after the X2 had been closed for more than a month, the detective sent a follow-up email to Park about the teen’s death.

“I never heard back from you regarding my previous email,” Nam wrote. “I saw news about multiple injuries involving the X2 ride at the Six Flags. Is there anything else I need to do?”

Park finally wrote back: “Apologies, I thought we responded.”

Park told the detective that since Christopher had died in a hotel room, there was no way to confirm which roller coasters the teen had ridden and “it would be difficult to determine which ride to assign this to or if it even is associated with a ride.”

Still, a few weeks later, state officials ordered a more sophisticated g-force test of the ride, citing a series of injuries and a death over the summer. CalOSHA said in a statement that there are limits to commonly used ride testing. The standard test focuses on the torso and does not “necessarily establish the full range of movement or physical impacts experienced by an individual rider, including the potential effects on the head and neck,” the agency said. The order for new g-force testing didn’t mention anyone by name, but it did refer to an incident on June 3, the day Christopher left the park with a headache and eventually retreated to his hotel room’s closet, where he died.

The test results are pending.

Later in September, Six Flags announced the ride’s permanent shuttering without acknowledging the injuries or deaths connected with the roller coaster. “While X2 consistently passed a multitude of safety tests, we have decided to close the ride because we believe it’s the right thing to do,” Magic Mountain president Brian Oerding said in a statement . “Ride safety is a cornerstone of our business, and when we see guest confidence affected, we take it seriously.”
