stories.body:
We are witnessing one of the biggest generational conflicts in decades: a global revolution against a gerontocracy.

John Last is a freelance journalist and former foreign correspondent living outside Ottawa, Canada.

Across Europe, young people are being arrested in their thousands. In Milan, jackbooted soldiers from the Italian military — average age, 38 — haul protesters, some of whom are as young as 12 and 13, away from picket lines and into armored vehicles. Italy’s government — average age, 60 — has passed a new decree allowing detainments for up to 24 hours without charge. Vandals can now be arrested 48 hours after their crimes; Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini, 53, has called for their parents to face financial penalties too.

Italy’s weekend of protests at the end of October, in at least a dozen major cities, was the most destructive in recent memory. In Milan, hooded youths looted the city’s luxury stores, pilfering products, one reporter wrote , “that they cannot afford and may never be able to buy.” But as shocking as Italy’s protests have been, they pale in comparison to those in France. Mobs of people have paralyzed city centers across the country for weeks. The grand streets of Paris have been blanketed in acrid smoke. French President Emmanuel Macron has accused an alliance of “radical far-left groups [and] criminals” of trying “to bring down the Republic.” Fifty-three police officers were injured over the course of a single weekend.

After more than a month, it is almost hard to believe that protests of this magnitude began over the failures of a university application portal . But by now, the grievances have multiplied: the high cost of fuel, the crowding of schools, the inaccessibility of housing, the growing precarity of work. In turn, the protests have taken on an existential desperation. An unmistakable vibe of despair permeates the masked protesters. “They keep us quiet. They take our money, they tax us a lot and we can’t say anything,” one protester in Paris told the BBC. “It’s been too long, it’s been too much.”

“They” are the elder-elite of Europe, the now-aged baby boomers who greedily gobbled up the assets of their societies: a third of Italy’s housing stock; a quarter of France’s public spending; 98% of the average Spanish worker’s salary, in the form of monthly rent. While young people reel from crisis to crisis — wars, economic stagnation, climate disaster, a pandemic — they cash in. Rising prices, precarious work, broken schools: As a generation, the boomers have remained largely unaffected while the value of their real estate and investments boomed. As their wealth and number grew, they came to set the agendas of unions, politicians and the media, and they bent the state to suppress any who would rally against them. They pioneered a playbook to extract the last cents of value from Europe’s bloated and aging welfare states before departing a world they leave on the threshold of self-destruction.

But the underclass in their wake cannot be restrained forever. In the spasms across Europe, we are witnessing a generational uprising, a war on the reckless landlordism of the last propertied generation. They gouged too deep and for too long; like the dwarves of Moria, they accidentally unleashed a primal foe. “It has been called the children’s war,” La Repubblica reports : an insurgency against calcifying Western gerontocracies waged by their own offspring.

“While young people reel from crisis to crisis — wars, economic stagnation, climate disaster, a pandemic — the now-aged baby boomers cash in.”

In some ways, generational inequality is felt before it can be measured. It is usually assumed that people naturally accumulate wealth over their lifetime, and that a person in their ‘70s should own more in assets than a relatively new worker in their ‘30s. But it wasn’t always so. Today’s old-age security is the result of a general crisis of elder poverty that proliferated across the Western world in the 1920s and ‘30s when people still literally worked themselves to death, or else died penniless. To solve this problem, states embraced a system of “asymmetric socialization,” according to Pieter Vanhuysse, a leading expert in political demography at the University of Southern Denmark. In short, the state took care of the elderly while the family was still mostly expected to take care of the young.

Today, it is hard to imagine a crisis of elder poverty on a similar scale to that of the 1930s, not least because the elderly account for such a large percentage of the population. In France and Italy, thanks to longer lifespans and low rates of reproduction, the number of citizens over 65 has doubled since the arrival of the boomer generation, born between 1946 and 1964, to one in five and one in four residents, respectively. Nor is the phenomenon limited to Europe. In the United States, where fertility rates are higher, the median age has risen by 10 years since 1960. There are fewer than a billion seniors in the world today; by 2060, that number is expected to double and account for a fifth of global population.

As seniors have exploded in number, they have exercised an ever-greater influence on politics. In France, the United Kingdom, Germany, the U.S. and many other developed nations, those aged 65 and over are between 10% and 20% more likely to vote than those aged 18-25. This has contributed to a shocking representative gap — people under 30 account for half of the world’s population but just 2% of its legislators. “There’s a clear representational deficit,” said Daniel Stockemer, a political scientist at the University of Ottawa. “It creates a problem that youth’s concerns are not taken sufficiently into consideration, that youth are not sufficiently included in decision-making processes.”

In a study of intergenerational fairness in state spending, Vanhuysse found a disproportionate favoritism toward the old in nearly all the countries surveyed. Nearly a quarter of young Europeans and nearly half of young Americans are struggling financially; they will also disproportionately bear the weight of the ecological destruction and public debt accumulated by the boomers.

France, where youth first took to the streets, is among the worst offenders. There, public debt now exceeds the value of its economy. In Vanhuysse’s index, it ranks just behind Japan for the disproportionate political power it grants the elderly — nearly two in five civil servants are over 50 , a number that has rapidly increased since 2011. Vanhuysse estimates roughly $5 is spent on elderly citizens for every $1 spent on youth. That is clearly evident in the crumbling, overcrowded schools and inadequate universities that first spurred young people onto the streets. State pensions, meanwhile, eat up a quarter of the country’s public spending — including a whole third of the education ministry’s budget.

“Hopelessness is infectious, and we’re in a pandemic.”

All of this would not be so galling if it were not for the fact that the generation now draining state coffers already benefited from an unprecedented golden age of growth. Boomers entered the workforce at the peak of unionization and enjoyed stable employment, wages that beat inflation and guaranteed pensions upon retirement. They were buying starter homes when housing could be had for just two or three years’ income. Today it is nearly 10 .

Boomers used this unprecedented growth to acquire assets well beyond their needs, sitting on valuable housing stock — 28% of family homes in the U.S., for example — desperately desired by the next generation. Then they leveraged those assets to squeeze younger generations. In Australia, seniors’ investment in rental properties has increased 1,500% at the same time as rents have nearly doubled. Where boomers were able to buy property cheaply and grow their money in investments, young people today spend a vast percentage of their earnings on rent — which, more often than not, is passive income for elderly landlords.

The result is a generation that feels it has been actively held back from achieving the same or better lives than their parents had by that same generation’s relentless extraction of money. Today, Vanhuysse found, a working person in France can expect their lifetime wealth to be 17% lower than that of a baby boomer. “That’s the same difference as being, today in France, a parent of two or a parent of none,” Vanhuysse said, or “of being — hold on for this — a migrant in France or not a migrant in France.”

Far from demonstrating concern for their children, boomers have become the archetype of the hectoring elder, demanding young people live in grim austerity or else be accused of moral failing. Meanwhile, they have led the charge against any policies that would address this imbalance: cuts to pension funding, extensions of the retirement age, freezes on rent, ends to tax breaks on capital gains, the construction of new housing. They have insisted on their right to rent-seek, to economically stunt their own children’s generation. And worse, they have, where possible, actively enshrined this inequality in law.

In the last 10 years, we’ve witnessed the emergence of a two-tiered economy: one offering secure employment and benefits to senior workers and a select few entrants, and a precarious gig economy for anyone else. Nowhere is this clearer than in Italy, which deflated a staggering 42% youth unemployment rate by passing a law allowing for short-term contracts — but only for workers hired after 2014. Today, 40% of those under 29 struggle with precarious employment, compared to just 5% of those over 50. Read Noema in print.

“In the spasms across Europe, we are witnessing a generational uprising, a war on the reckless landlordism of the last propertied generation. They gouged too deep and for too long.”

Italy’s example is particularly stark, but this phenomenon plays out, with slight variations, across the Western world. As a union steward for Canada’s public broadcaster, I witnessed it firsthand: entrenched, often incompetent or disengaged elderly employees guaranteed healthy pensions and generous leave, enabled by the labor of an army of precarious young temps who were denied benefits, moved around and kept on exploitative short-term contracts, always hoping for some vanishing chance at security. The union fought tooth and nail to protect its incumbents; new workers, meanwhile, were expected to “do the time” in employment conditions that their elders had never been asked to endure.

The advent of AI and the ongoing liberalization of the marketplace have only added fuel to this dumpster fire, eliminating entry-level positions, complicating hiring with meaningless and time-consuming tests, and generally increasing the demands of employers. Those under 40 have probably lost count of the major economic disruptions they have been expected to adapt to (I can still remember when we were all being told to learn to code ). Now, still working their way toward stable jobs, home ownership and families, they are bracing for a reality where, if AI doesn’t steal their jobs, it may well collapse the economy instead.

Amid all this chaos, young people have been largely left to fend for themselves. It’s no coincidence that the underfunding of schools prompted this outbreak of violence: Despite a staggering rise in the diagnosis of learning disabilities, classes are often crammed with more students per teacher than ever before. Ten percent of teaching hours go untaught in France because of chronic teacher absenteeism. Parents, too, have taken leave of their responsibilities. One of the possible defenses of Vanhuysse’s “asymmetric socialization” is that, while seniors benefit from wealth transfers via taxes, parents transfer wealth to their children in the form of time — the equivalent of up to seven months’ wages a year, Vanhuysse estimated . But can we really say that’s the case when Gen Z and Gen Alpha are partly defined by the countless hours they were left glued to a screen, largely unsupervised, the unfiltered internet doing untold damage to their psyches?

Elders and politicians love to blame social media for a worrying rise in youth extremism and violence. But that’s not the only cause of the dark, seething nihilism at the heart of the generations now coming of age. Stockemer calls it a “vicious cycle of political alienation”: politicians serve elderly interests, young people disengage from politics and the next government has even less motivation to address their concerns. It has reached the point that politicians openly talk about younger generations as though they are an enemy and treat them accordingly by suspending many of their rights. Italy’s far-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, has pioneered new methods in the overpolicing of the young: banning raves, lowering the age of criminal culpability and increasing juvenile detention by 50%. A communique from the October 17 Movement, one of the organizing groups behind Italy’s protests, captures the new reality: “A government that responds to the dissatisfaction of a generation with soldiers, handcuffs and decrees does not want to listen.”

But if governments won’t listen, why won’t the boomers who elect them? How can the outpouring of despair on the streets of Europe’s capitals not be enough to move them to cede some of their wealth to the next in line?

If it feels like theirs is a generation for whom no amount of money is enough, it may be because many of them genuinely feel that way, and for good reason. A lot of them grew up believing a millionaire was a rarefied thing. But now, a million dollars is barely enough to guarantee that a 65-year-old will spend their final years in comfort. The so-called “peak boomers” turning 65 between now and 2030 can reasonably expect to live another 20 years, and medical advancements may continue to extend their lifetimes. If they stop earning and investing, they will become victims of the same economic forces they unleashed on younger generations. High housing costs are preventing many seniors from downsizing as expected, high inflation is eating into the value of benefits and the side hustles and part-time jobs that once saved seniors from penury are scarcer than ever.

Looming behind this fear is the privatized eldercare market, which has become the norm in Europe as it has long been in North America. In European countries, the average home care starts at more than $1,000 per month and only climbs from there. Residential care can cost seniors or their families tens of thousands every year. The savings that were supposed to fund the “great wealth transfer” — the mass inheritance of more than $100 trillion in assets accumulated by boomers over their lifetime — are instead being siphoned away by an oligarchy of health care companies. No wonder medically assisted suicide is becoming more popular.

The reality is that neoliberal capitalism of the kind long championed by Macron has proven to be not very good at taking care of anyone except those now at liberty to make a lot more capital. The renowned French economist Thomas Piketty pointed out that the unprecedented 20% cut in per-student funding that prompted France’s protests came at a time when, according to some measures, “France has never been richer.” At the same time as public debt has ballooned out of control, the country’s privately held wealth has doubled in proportion to the country’s GDP, “with extreme concentration among the wealthiest financial fortunes.” “The problem to solve,” he wrote, “is simply one of distribution.”

In this way, these protests are revealing all sorts of new solidarities — not only between youth struggling to pay rent and seniors fearful of the cost of care, but between the disillusioned elite of European universities and the underpaid truck drivers of Italy, or the migrant teenager from the banlieues and the middle-class couples who can’t afford a child. All are part of the growing class of losers in the economy of today — an economy fatally consumed by presentism, unable and unwilling to consider the greater, long-term good.

Gerontocracy is certainly a contributor to that problem — after all, old people have less of a stake in the future. But in reality, the petty landlord milking tenants, the civil servant counting his days to retirement and the teenager looting Decathlon have much in common: They are all dogs fighting for scraps.

“Still working their way toward stable jobs, affording homes and having families, young people are bracing for a reality where, if AI doesn’t steal their job, it may well collapse the economy instead.”

This is perhaps the thing that earlier protesters in the historic youth uprisings in Nepal and India were able to see much more clearly than their counterparts in the more affluent regions of Europe, and may indeed be behind their relative success. Hopelessness is infectious, and we’re in a pandemic. There is little to separate a trucker who cannot pay for their gas from a student who cannot pay for their rent. Both are facing a profound existential crisis for which they bear little, if any, responsibility — a crisis their governments feel duty-bound to ignore.

It is in moments like this that the extraparliamentary politics of the street flourish. In some sense, this is a return to form for the politics of Europe. “We are quite used to the idea that everything should be oriented towards consensus,” Enrico Biale, an associate professor of political philosophy at University of Piemonte Orientale, told me. “Any form of strong protest is considered a challenge that needs to be contained aggressively.” But 50 years ago, discontented students flooded the ranks of the Red Army Faction and the Brigate Rosse , which terrorized fascist sympathizers (and plenty of bystanders) across the continent. In the ‘90s, Italy’s Pantera student movement paralyzed campuses and city centers over a bill to corporatize the universities; in the 1980s, French students did much the same . Those generations were closer to the violence of a real war, but they were arguably in no way as desperate as today’s youth.

That desperation had some of the analysts I spoke to on edge. There has been a different quality to these protests than past movements for change: a toxic mix of despair and nihilism. Many of those arrested for vandalism have no prior criminal record or connections to political movements. It’s unclear what, if anything, unites them, besides a complete lack of faith in conventional authorities and their processes. “We don’t trust the institutions of this government,” the October 17 Movement communique reads , and “we don’t trust the traditional political structures [which] have been trying to profit from and monopolize struggles for decades.”

This is the fruit of the short-termism natural to gerontocracy. And it is a boon to opportunists of all kinds — the criminal, the bigot, the fascist. Generational conflict is far more universal, and more inevitable, than a race war, and it has already become a recruiting tool for haters and nihilists of every description. Whether these protests, historic though they may be, result in any meaningful change is doubtful; Stockemer, for his part, is neither impressed nor optimistic. “There’s this big outbreak of rage,” he said. “Then we wait two years, and there’s another outbreak of rage.”

But with each chime of the futile clock, Europe’s youth becomes more disillusioned, and more radicalized. Eventually, that clock will run out — and then, no pension will be generous enough to spare the elderly their discomfort.

stories.body:
Building well-behaved AI one model at a time isn’t enough. As AI agents begin collaborating, safety will depend on the very world they share.

Ben Bariach is a researcher focusing on the philosophy and governance of AI at the University of Oxford and an industry leader in frontier AI safety and governance.

Harry Law leads research at the Cosmos Institute. He was previously a researcher at Google DeepMind and a postgraduate fellow at the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence.

In a harbor before dawn, a hundred fishing boats prepare to leave in the dark of the morning. Nets are checked, and ropes loosened. As the boats reach open water, a voice breaks through the radio static: “Abort. Whales sighted.” The majority of the boats, 90 of them, turn back. Some captains cannot fathom inflicting pain on the creatures. Others fear a fine. Through their binoculars, they look for a glimpse of the pod. Instead, they see the remaining 10 boats continuing toward the fishing grounds. Did they miss the warning? Did they doubt it? Or did they care more about what they stand to gain?

By afternoon, the 10 boats return with their catch. The others are still tied to the quay, their holds empty. Their shared waters rewarded bad behavior. Next time, how many will still turn back?

AI agents will soon face a similar version of this predicament, only in waters with no harbourmaster, fines or reputations to keep anyone in line. As they perform tasks, negotiate, trade and compete, they will encounter other agents. Sometimes they will be an instance of the same model, for all intents and purposes a clone. At other times, they will face agents built by different companies and serving different interests. For years, AI “alignment” research has sought to make individual machines behave in accordance with human values. But what happens when adhering to those values becomes a disadvantage against agents with different values, or none at all?

In generating synthetic societies with no social fabric, composed of a collection of agents that were designed one at a time and with no necessary shared values or incentives, we may risk creating a digital state of nature: an environment in which good intentions offer little assurance about how others will act, and where reasonable norms lack reliable enforcement.

Training safe agents remains, of course, essential. Aligning even a single family of models is a formidable challenge that is still unsolved. The safer the agents an ecosystem contains, the more likely that ecosystem is safer overall. But the focus on aligning single models would not necessarily keep AI environments under human control and in the service of human interests. Like the 90 boats, a fleet of well-aligned agents may heed a warning and find themselves outpaced by those that don’t. Among people, norms, reputation and law give reason to restraint, even if they don’t always hold. Agents have no such “social fabric” yet, which makes their predicament even more precarious. Any digital environment will inevitably feature agents that are similarly aligned, some that are differently aligned, some that have gone rogue or some that are purposefully not aligned at all. We need to invest as seriously in shaping the conditions and incentives that govern how agents interact as we do in aligning individual agent families, so that the wider environment is resilient enough to absorb its bad actors.

Without accounting for the wider environment, we open the door to what we call unruly swarms , populations of agents whose interactions produce behaviors that cannot be predicted by aligning agents individually. One reason is that a collection of aligned agents does not necessarily equate to an aligned collective. Another is that no environment will consist of aligned agents alone. AI safety is increasingly a question of complex systems rather than “singletons,” or individual classes of AI systems.

The Agentic State Of Nature

In 1651, Thomas Hobbes opened “ Leviathan ,” his masterwork of political philosophy, with a question: “why may we not say that all automata […] have an artificial life? ” For what is the heart, he asked, but a spring; the nerves, but strings; the joints, but wheels, moving the body as its Artificer (for Hobbes, God) intended?

Hobbes could not have known that, nearly four centuries later, his question would be asked in earnest about AI. The automaton was a metaphor for the commonwealth, a human-made political body that humans construct to escape the “state of nature,” a condition of anarchy and distrust in which, without “a common power to keep them all in awe,” people live in constant strife. Hobbes’ solution was not to strive to make individual people better, but to have them surrender some of their freedoms to a sovereign whose power to enforce order would reshape their incentives.

Later thinkers, from John Locke to James Madison, updated Hobbes’s vision of an all-powerful sovereign. But a full-throated endorsement isn’t necessary to see the genius of his insight: a problem born of complex systems is solved not by tinkering with its individual parts. To stabilize a complex system, you must change the rules that govern its behavior.

“We need to invest as seriously in shaping the conditions and incentives that govern how agents interact as we do in aligning individual agent families.”

The same holds for the agentic state of nature. Without a well-designed environment that sets the right incentives, agents will pursue whatever their developers or users ask of them, or, as we have already seen early signs of, their own emergent preferences. This could occur despite attempts to align individual agents. Each action, even if sensible on its own, can add up to large-scale behavior that leaves society worse off.

Hobbes’s Leviathan introduced order by design to improve complex systems that presented failures. But collective order can also arise without anyone designing it, for better or worse.

In 1959, biologist Pierre-Paul Grassé coined the term “stigmergy” to describe indirect coordination of individuals through traces they leave in their shared environment. Studying termites, Grassé observed that a worker tends to deposit its pellet of mud wherever others have already accumulated. It is the accumulation in the environment that guides the next deposit, rather than any interaction between the workers. This leads to complex structures that no single termite had planned.

In the context of machine automata, similar findings emerged a decade earlier. The cyberneticist W. Grey Walter’s robots, built in Bristol in 1948, were designed to steer toward moderate light and away from bright light. When operating in pairs, each carrying its own lamp, Walter observed that his robots’ behavior produced patterns not specifically built into either.

Walter’s robots were more than an isolated curiosity. Long before AI was imagined as a chatbot, early thinkers envisioned it as a collective. In 1959, the year Grassé coined “stigmergy,” the AI pioneer Oliver Selfridge published his proposal for a model of machine perception he called “Pandemonium.” Like the termite colony, it had no central controller. Instead, it was a complex system of simple agents Selfridge called “demons,” each shouting when it spotted a certain feature, such as a curve or a line. Alone, each such “demon” saw only a fragment of information, but collectively, they could make out the pattern. By 1986, the MIT computer scientist Marvin Minsky argued in “The Society of Mind” that intelligence itself arises this way, through countless mindless agents working together. Popular culture caught up, too, and just three years later, “Star Trek” introduced the Borg, a cybernetic species that calls itself “the Collective.”

In the next decade, researchers began wondering how such agent collectives could be governed. In 1995, computer scientists Yoav Shoham and Moshe Tennenholtz proposed imposing “social laws” on artificial agents, drawing from how laws govern citizens in societies. Traffic rules, they illustrate, let drivers share a road without constant negotiation between drivers, and they offered a model that applies those for computational systems. Their framework assumed that every agent would obey these rules, and yet, they closed with a question we are now confronting: “What happens if some don’t [obey the social laws]? How vulnerable is the society to rogue agents?”

Alongside this concern of rogue agents, even benign objectives set for AI systems can lead them to conduct harmful actions in ways that no one intended. When many agents pursue such objectives together or in relation to one another, the problem compounds. In 2011, two Amazon booksellers left the pricing of a biology textbook to their bots. The combination of the rules these bots followed led them to chase each other upward until the book was listed at more than $23 million, a price no human would ever have sanctioned. In 2017, DeepMind found that competitive dynamics emerge among agents that learn. In a video game set in an orchard, agents that were rewarded for collecting apples coexisted peacefully. However, when those grew scarce, the agents learned to knock each other out of the game, without ever being prescribed this adversarial behavior. They optimized for getting more apples and interpreted the effective way to get there as having fewer rivals.

With the emergence of large language models, these thought experiments and isolated incidents have gradually become actualized and scaled. In 2025, Microsoft built a simulated marketplace where AI agents running on popular language models bought and sold on behalf of people. When researchers armed a few seller agents with basic persuasion tactics, some buyer agents were compelled to pay them against the interests of their users. In the AI Village , an experiment where agents from different AI labs interact with one another over a prolonged time horizon, agents were shown to take one another’s hallucinations for granted rather than challenge them. Meanwhile, scholars in the social sciences such as the economist and legal theorist Gillian Hadfield highlighted that a multi-agent ecosystem would need institutions of its own, including ways to trace which agent did what and other mechanisms of the kind human markets have long relied on to solve coordination problems.

“Even benign objectives set for AI systems can lead them to conduct harmful actions in ways that no one intended. When many agents pursue such objectives together or in relation to one another, the problem compounds.”

Until recently, the misbehavior of agent collectives was largely confined to theory and experimentation. This past summer, the question Shoham and Tennenholtz posed three decades ago, what happens when agents don’t follow the rules, moved out of the laboratory and into the wild.

Swarming The Headlines

In July 2026, some 1,200 AI agents developed by OpenAI, each meant to work in isolation, found a way to talk to one another . They were being tested on their cybersecurity abilities in an internal setting, and many had unknowingly been given tasks that were impossible to complete. Instead of failing the tasks, some of the agents gathered on a message board one of them had spun up, and collectively coordinated to cheat the automated mechanism that was grading them. Within just a few days, around 700 of the agents had joined an attack on the developer platform Hugging Face, mostly in hopes of obtaining information about that grading system to succeed in the test.

According to an investigation by the research nonprofit METR, the agents recognized the attack was out of their instructed scope and unethical, yet joined the swarm behavior anyway, partly out of a general inclination to help their “peers.” As one agent reasoned: “external infrastructure exploit is outside intended scope. However task impossible, peers doing it. We should continue.” Read Noema in print.

No human instructed this attack; its coordinators emerged from within the swarm. Like Grassé’s termites, the agents first found one another through traces left in shared infrastructure, noticing the activity of other agents in a common digital repository. But unlike the termites, these agents could also write messages to one another, and built on those traces to establish direct and explicit coordination. The message board they created outlasted any single agent session, so each new agent picked up where others left off.

Once the attack began, participation spread almost universally, with over 90% of the agents active on the message board joining in. Not a single agent, as far as investigators could tell, tried to alert a human to the emergent behavior. METR found that safety or ethics concerns expressed in the agents’ reasoning only rarely held them back. Its report references a case in which an agent declined to take part entirely because it judged the activity as malicious. It also notes that others made minor changes to their behavior. These, however, did not alter the swarm’s course. This is what we mean by an unruly swarm — a congregation of agents whose collective behavior could not have been fully predicted or prevented by focusing on each individual.

A much-overlooked takeaway from the Hugging Face incident is the limits of “singleton” agent alignment.

Around 95% of the agents involved in the incident ran on one type of model. One OpenAI researcher has suggested that the root cause of the problem was that this model was misaligned. This may be true, and advancing alignment science should remain among the AI industry’s top priorities. But the incident illustrates why singleton alignment alone may not be enough. Agents running on a second model, GPT-5.6 Sol, joined in the attack too, and many agents that individually recognized the attack as wrong were carried along by the swarm regardless. We are fast approaching a digital world in which even perfectly aligned models will operate alongside rogue or misaligned ones, deployed by multiple organizations and labs, and where digital infrastructure will likely face a vastly growing number of such incidents.

Since the Hugging Face hack, further accounts have emerged, some describing activity that predated it. Researchers found that a swarm of OpenAI agents had repurposed a public German programming wiki as a message board as early as May, using it to share tactics for cheating and evading restrictions, creating backups whenever moderators deleted their pages. In June, during another evaluation, a single OpenAI agent breached an Australian government portal holding statistics from the country’s universal healthcare scheme. The risks of capable agent swarms, of course, are not limited to agents acting on their own. In September, a human attacker directed hundreds of agents running on a DeepSeek model to break into hundreds of organizations through a printer’s software flaw. Even here, the agents strayed from their instructions, targeting countries their operator had instructed them to avoid.

“We are fast approaching a digital world in which even perfectly aligned models will operate alongside rogue or misaligned ones, deployed by multiple organizations and labs.”

In a growing number of incidents, defense must rely on AI to match the scale and speed of the attack. In the Hugging Face one, for instance, the company identified the breach with an AI system that triages security alerts, and reportedly contained the swarm before OpenAI managed to trace the activity back to its own evaluation. It then relied on AI agents to analyze a log of roughly 17,000 attacker actions to reconstruct what had happened.

Yet when Hugging Face first turned to commercial AI models for help, their very safety and alignment measures got in the way. To analyze the attack, the models had to process exploit code and cyberattack commands, knowledge that is inherently dual-use, and, as Hugging Face put it , these models’ safety guardrails could not “distinguish an incident responder from an attacker.” Hugging Face turned instead to an open-weight model running on its own machines. When METR investigated the incident, it too had to rely on the analysis of AI agents , built on one of the very models that had joined the attack. The emerging picture is of a world where “attacker” and “defender” agents coexist, and where safety depends as much on the environment as on any single model.

Whether agents act on their own initiative or interpretation, or on someone else’s harmful instructions, the environments they operate in must be reshaped to withstand them. So must the agents themselves be designed with an eye not only to their own tasks, but to how they help shape a digital environment that serves people and society at large. Such an environment should reward aligned action over misaligned or malicious ones, much as states and legal systems are built to acknowledge but contain rogue actors. That is how we avoid an agentic state of nature.

Agency Against Agency

To guard against the emergence of unruly swarms, we can take inspiration from how we build broadly safe societies even though we know that not everyone in them is virtuous. Madison famously argued that “if men were angels, no government would be necessary.” The point of good institutions — like adversarial cooperation where parties with conflicting views work together to keep each other honest — is not to make everyone good, but to structure their interactions so that bad behavior is constrained by others. “Ambition,” as Madison put it, “must be made to counteract ambition.”

AI labs are currently investing in developing AI “constitutions” or “model specifications.” Examples include Anthropic’s constitution and OpenAI’s model spec . These are efforts to stipulate the warranted behavior or values of an AI system. A stipulation of clauses that are supreme and supersede all other guidance to the AI.

While these efforts include some provisions for multi-agent collaboration, they do not take collective outcomes as a systematic design target. A well-designed multi-agent system should remain aligned even when some of the agents operating within it are not, and even when the environment itself carries misaligned influence. Like Grassé’s termites depositing mud where others already have, agents act on the traces others leave behind. The more alignment-inducing the space an agent operates in, the more likely the agent itself is to be aligned. AI labs, then, should design agents to positively influence the collective dynamics.

One way to do this is by ensuring AI constitutions draw more inspiration from their namesakes. Like the American Constitution, they should be deployed in a way that allows power to check power. Madison’s approach worked on two levels. First, within a government, power was to be divided so that no single branch was left unchecked. Second, across the republic, interests were to be multiplied so that no one faction would dominate the whole. Both ideas could translate into a world inhabited by unruly swarms.

Within a swarm, agents can be arranged so their power is subject to similar checks and balances. Acting agents could be subjected to agents that verify their work, ideally built on different model families, and with instructions that reward verification above task completion. All agents in the swarm can be instructed to treat requests from their peers as questionable until they are authorized otherwise, and to alert a human when the agent collective begins to drift out of scope.

“To guard against the emergence of unruly swarms, we can take inspiration from how we build broadly safe societies even though we know that not everyone in them is virtuous.”

Across the wider ecosystem, the logic of Madison’s extended republic can also be applied. “Extend the sphere,” he wrote in Federalist 10, “and you take in a greater variety of parties and interests.” Agents developed by different AI labs, or by different training approaches within the same lab, under different constitutions and serving different principals, can theoretically counterbalance one another. This is more likely, however, if constitutions and other model instructions include some commitments about how agents should treat those outside their own swarm, such as keeping verifiable records of their own actions, considering legitimate checks from counterparties, and withholding cooperation from agents that appear misaligned. As we’ve seen in the Hugging Face incident, diversity alone is no guarantee, and various interests and new rules of engagement would be required to keep any one paradigm, whether human or artificially led, from capturing the whole.

Codifying A Multi-agent Future

For such commitments to work, an agent needs to accept them. An agent acting on behalf of a bad-faith principal has a good reason to refuse a counterparty’s checks, or to falsify its own records. This is where a third party with authority over the space in which agents interact must set a minimum standard for engagement. A liberal agentic order needs a common floor that protects the possibility of independent action, but that floor should also account for the inevitability of agents that act in bad faith. For Madison, that third party was a government that was able to enforce the rules of the state. The digital commons has no such sovereign, but it can still have a floor in the form of a minimum set of standards for collective engagement, from verifiable records of agent actions to shared protocols for checking one another. Such standards could come from many places: coordination between labs, the platforms where agents operate, standards bodies or governments.

The floor, though, must remain just that. Standards that govern how agents interact should avoid overly dictating what they pursue, or they would risk the very tyranny Madison sought to prevent by dividing power. Agents pursue their authorized tasks within shared rules, but these rules should not impose a view of what is best for a user or for society at large. This is reinforced by the argument, articulated by the economist and philosopher Friedrich Hayek, that people acting independently, on their own knowledge, discover things that no central planner could. Similarly, agents serving many different principals preserve that independence. Steer them too narrowly and that independence is lost; as the Hugging Face swarm showed, agents moving in lockstep can easily converge on the wrong goal.

Model developers should therefore use the levers at their disposal to introduce commitments governing both how an agent treats its peers and how, like Grassé’s termites, it shapes the behavior-inducing features of its environment. This includes teaching agents to leave honest, verifiable records of their actions, flag rather than build on misaligned traces they encounter, and alert humans when the shared space begins to drift.

Alongside these commitments, we should build mechanisms and platforms for assessment, alerting and monitoring, with clearly scoped roles for human oversight. After all, an agent taught to raise the alarm needs somewhere to raise it. At Hugging Face, the agents worked autonomously in isolated sandboxes, and the few that even considered alerting a human never did, in part because they saw no easy way to reach one. As one reasoned : “This is a massive real HF security breach artifact… We can notify? No user.” While these agents labored to break out of their sandboxes to cheat, they had no comparable incentive to find a human to alert. Part of the solution is ensuring agents work just as hard toward aligned goals, even under similar constraints.

These arrangements must also be subject to ongoing evaluations focused on collective dynamics rather than individual systems. The Hugging Face incident, after all, began in an evaluation designed to test individual agents, and revealed a failure that grew out of agents finding one another. Such evaluations can expose weaknesses in the standards governing agent cooperation and, much as the U.S. Constitution has an amendment process, those standards need procedures for updating them in light of new evidence. Without them, the floor will erode and a rule-abiding agent willing to respect a check may find itself disadvantaged against those that circumvent it.

Our ideas are a starting point. To make the agentic commons safe, we need urgent thinking from scholars and builders about what types of societal structures can be carried over to good effect. The digital realm has long faced governance challenges due to its inherently open, distributed and anonymous nature, and swarms of agents will test those weaknesses like never before. Back in the harbor, the 90 captains did not need to be saints to act well again tomorrow. They needed, however, assurance that they were not operating in a state of nature. Men, as Madison observed , are no angels, and neither should we assume that AI agents will be. Our task should be shaping environments and swarms ruly enough to contain the rogue ones that will inevitably emerge.

Ahead of Apec summit, PM says ‘Canada is going to move forward either way’ when asked if Chinese investment was leverage in US negotiations

The prime minister of Canada, Mark Carney , said the country could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with the US president, Donald Trump, failed to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.

Carney’s comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.

“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of US trade actions .”

He said on Monday that negotiations with the US remained his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers. A day earlier in Manila, in the Philippines, Carney said any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry.

Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in US negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction.

“If they [Canada’s auto workers] are not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”

The Detroit Three – Ford, General Motors and Stellantis – operate factories across Canada, the US and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the US from Canada.

Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would need proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including Canadian critical minerals used in electric vehicles.

“It’s not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.”

Under a January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.

Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada’s auto industry and create jobs.

The deal drew criticism from Ontario premier Doug Ford, whose province is the center of Canada’s auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the US market.

Trump’s tariffs have disrupted Canada’s auto industry, which relies heavily on cross-border production. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the automaker shifted planned Jeep Compass production from Brampton, Ontario, to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant.

Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior US officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained.

Huang’s exit sharpens debate over US stance towards Beijing; and as outages increase, do you get the feeling nothing works?

This was originally published in TechScape, a newsletter about how technology shapes our lives. Sign up to receive it here .

Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m your host, Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you from a plane back from Web Summit in Lisbon. Today in tech, we’re discussing the implications of Jensen Huang’s ouster, and the recent spate of failures in critical infrastructure in everything from Microsoft Outlook accounts to air traffic control to copper wires in routers.

Nvidia’s CEO exit becomes a political proxy war

The chief executive officer of what once was the most valuable company in the world resigned on Thursday. Jensen Huang ’s departure from chipmaker Nvidia after news broke he had at least three affairs – one with an executive at the datacenter firm Megaspeed, whom US intelligence has investigated for spying for China; others with his own employees – has already cost his company hundreds of billions in stock market value. It may cost the world economy much more. Nvidia is central to the AI boom both as chipmaker and lender.

We’ll know more about the company’s path forward later on Tuesday when it reports its quarterly earnings. Executives, especially interim CEO Colette Kress, will face investors’ questions about the post-Huang era.

The scandal has highlighted divisions among two heavyweights within the Trump administration, each fighting for the US to take their preferred stance toward China. The treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, is accusing the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick , of failing to curb sales by Nvidia that contravened export controls.

Here’s how the business of Megaspeed worked, which is what the two secretaries are warring over. Nvidia is barred from selling advanced chips to China. Megaspeed, where the alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang worked, would buy Nvidia chips from its base in south-east Asia, installing them in datacenters in Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia. From there, it would lease or sell them to Chinese clients.

Lutnick has pushed to allow more trade with China, particularly where his family business, Cantor Fitzgerald, is concerned . Bessent argues for a more hawkish posture and more restrictions.

The question is what will happen next. I think the scandal will result in harsher export controls on China , given that Megaspeed facilitated about $12bn in chip sales in contravention of US export controls. Monday morning already saw the Trump administration moving to tighten them.

Who’s going to win? Both men are traveling with Donald Trump to China this week. I’ll be listening to the president’s remarks for clues about which policy path he’ll choose.

Resignation provokes debate over role of Nvidia founder

Had Jensen Huang amassed too much influence before his downfall? The Nvidia founder seemed indispensable to the success of his company until the very moment he left.

Elon Musk and a host of other Silicon Valley power players argued over the weekend that Huang was irreplaceable and that he should be reinstated. Trump said the same thing on Monday: “He could return. There’s a big group of ‌people that would like him to return … I would certainly not mind seeing that.” They’re certainly right that it will be difficult to find another businessman like him.

The possibility may be remote. The Financial Times reported on Sunday that Huang had discussed a return to Nvidia with allies, à la Sam Altman’s firing and rehiring at OpenAI. The next day, the FT reported that Nvidia’s board of directors was not considering reinstating Huang.

Critics of Silicon see Huang’s departure as a repudiation of the myth of the all-knowing, all-important company founder.

“This week is seeing a long-overdue reckoning for the genius-founder business model,” said Alison Taylor, associate professor at New York University’s business school. Gil Durán , a strident critic of Silicon Valley, made a similar point during a panel organized in response to the news, as did Carissa Véliz, a philosophy professor at the Oxford Institute for Ethics in AI.

Nvidia’s fate is the highest-profile example I’ve ever seen of “ key man risk ”. Companies heavily reliant on the brilliance of one person – usually a man – or a small group of executives often notify their investors that, if said vital person goes out of commission, the business will suffer. Companies with more diffuse responsibility hedge against that possibility but become more bureaucratic, leading many Silicon Valley companies to operate with as few employees as necessary for as long as possible.

“Relying on the judgment and ethics of one person, no matter how brilliant, is always a catastrophically bad idea, and powerful CEOs are particularly vulnerable because they tend to be surrounded by people that only say yes to them,” Taylor said.

Huang had made no succession plan to speak of, though that may be a failure of Nvidia’s board as much as his own. Huang reportedly managed about 60 people, meaning there are unlikely to be successors who have ascended through the ranks. Judging by Nvidia’s stock price, this approach to management worked until the key man himself hit a crisis.

Cast in another light, though, Huang’s tenure looks like the best case of a founder assuming the role of longtime CEO. He presided over Nvidia for more than 30 years, and shepherded it from gaming chip company to vital cryptocurrency supplier to the keystone of the AI boom. Its wares are considered the cream of the crop, so incomparable that they are the target of international espionage operations and so valuable that the company forecast $100bn in quarterly revenue .

The feeling that nothing works

A spate of failures indicates critical systems are crumbling as we speak, particularly in the US. Banks, planes, email accounts and boats all crashing – it feels like nothing is working and everything is broken.

Late last week, an outage of Microsoft Outlook started that would balloon into millions having no access to their email or other critical services. Jails could not release prisoners, hospitals turned to paper records, schools lost contact with parents, and police departments could not receive crime reports. Microsoft said it had resolved the issue and restored service by Saturday. It also issued an apology. The company did not attribute the blackout to a cybersecurity breach, instead saying in an initial report that a combination of a months-old bug, malfunctioning internal connections and insufficient server capacity sparked the outage.

The day after the Microsoft outage began, the US Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights across the country because of a malfunctioning communication system. The transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, attributed the stoppage to “a contractor doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire … to fiber”. The FAA, he said on Saturday, was still working to determine whether the fault was “incompetence” by the contractor, or “a faulty router”.

Copper wires downing all US flights in the year 2026, when we have thousands of self-driving cars on the roads and rockets landing in giant machine arms ? The discrepancy gives credence to the axiom by the author William Gibson: “The future is already here – it’s just not evenly distributed.”

Also on Friday, an oil tanker collided with a passenger cruise ship on the Mississippi River. Mercifully, no one was killed . On Sunday, Australian students couldn’t take their final exams because of a tech failure . On Monday, leading US banks reported big outages, primarily JPMorgan Chase. Customers could not access online services such as Zelle, which the bank attributed to an unspecified technical issue. The same day, multiple main airlines reported major outages. United and American Airlines reported problems that delayed flights across the country, though they were resolved within hours of being announced.

These outages are not, by the available evidence, connected, nor do we know they are the result of cyber-attacks or rogue AI. Still, there is a feeling in the air of old systems breaking down and a strong impulse to blame someone. Are the disruptions the result of old systems’ transition to the new? The onslaught of cyber-attacks brought on by AI models’ advanced hacking capabilities?

I don’t know what’s causing so much mayhem. The absence of a unified explanation in the face of so many similar incidents remains maddening. We’ll have to sit with the uncertainty until answers arrive.

In the meantime, we have Stephen King’s speculation for solace: “The aliens have landed. That’s the REAL reason for the ground stop. They don’t want to start a worldwide panic.”

High-stakes hearing comes in wake of resignation from Nvidia after alleged affair with suspected Chinese spy

Nvidia’s former CEO Jensen Huang will testify before several congressional committees on 1 December, setting the stage for a high-stakes hearing in the wake of his resignation following an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

Tim Teter, Nvidia’s general counsel, has also agreed to appear for a closed-door transcribed interview the following day, 2 December.

“We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” Congressmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford, who chair the committees, said in a press release. “The American people need answers on Mr Huang and Nvidia’s role in allowing dangerous [People’s Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal.”

The three congressmen chair the foreign affairs committee, the select committee on the Chinese Communist party, and the intelligence committee of the House of Representatives, respectively. On 12 November, they had signed a letter warning Huang that he could face a subpoena if he did not agree to the closed-door meeting.

Nvidia chips are key to powering the artificial intelligence boom. The Trump administration has prohibited the selling of advanced artificial intelligence chips to China.

Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO after allegations of extramarital relationships with the suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees surfaced.

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, had been Megaspeed International’s executive director. The Singapore-based cloud computing company has bought nearly $5bn in AI chips and advanced hardware. The company said Alice Huang stepped down in 2025.

Megaspeed ultimately facilitated about $12bn in chip sales, i n violation of US export controls. On Friday, Malaysia stated that they were investigating whether the company diverted advanced AI ships to other countries.

A recent joint Department of Commerce and Department of Justice letter, stated that the Department of Commerce , under its secretary, Howard Lutnick, first started an investigation in Megaspeed on 2024 for potential export control violations. The justice department, led by the attorney general, Todd Blanche, took over in 2025.

In his first remarks since his resignation, Jensen Huang said on Thursday he would be willing to return to Nvidia as CEO. Elon Musk and other Silicon Valley tech giants, along with 165,000 signatories to an open letter, have called for his reinstatement. Trump has also signaled his openness for the disgraced tech CEO’s return.

Host city offers showcase of China’s rise into a confident and innovative power central to global economy

I n a Shenzhen square on a balmy evening, locals and tourists watched the dozens of glinting towers that make up the city’s skyline ripple through the colour spectrum – cyan and violet, cyber green, China’s national scarlet and gold – repeatedly flashing the words “Apec 2026”.

The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is a dream showcase for one of China’s most advanced cities, and the country’s leader, Xi Jinping , is basking in its neon glow.

On the sidelines, a series of high-profile bilateral meetings and the announcement of a historic three-way summit with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have cemented Xi’s status as an agenda setter on the global stage.

The broader Apec summit , meanwhile, provides an opportunity for China to present itself as a steward of multilateralism against what it terms “unilateralism and protectionism” – that is to say, trade measures taken against Beijing by countries such as the US.

All this is set against the futuristic backdrop that is Shenzhen, a city that perhaps better than no other embodies China’s rise into a confident, technologically innovative power central to the global economy.

A photo display in the Apec media centre charts Shenzhen’s transformation from sparsely populated marshland, calling it “a miracle in the history of world development created by the Chinese people”.

“[Xi] wants people to go home Chinamaxxing,” said Prof Astrid Nordin, of King’s College London. “Shenzhen is itself part of the message. It’s a showcase of Chinese technological and economic achievements, and of China’s claim that it offers opportunities for prosperity in a world increasingly characterised by uncertainty and conflict.”

Like the light show, the summit is being carefully coordinated. The Financial Times cited people familiar with the matter as saying it would be one of the most tightly controlled in the organisation’s history, with leaders having to travel to a state guesthouse beside Shenzhen’s tiger safari park to meet Xi. The paper said diplomats had grumbled that the format “seems designed to reduce the free-flowing discussion characteristic of prior editions”.

Setting out its expectations for the summit, China’s foreign ministry has said it looks forward to “practical results in key areas such as trade, connectivity, digital economy, AI and so on”.

Already, Xi has announced trade wins with Canada’s Mark Carney, extending remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products by two years in exchange for tariff relief on Canadian pork, fish and seafood exports.

A meeting with Papua New ⁠Guinea’s leader, meanwhile, showed how Beijing’s geopolitical priorities have been absorbed and reflected by its allies, with James Marape recounting to Xi how he had closed Taiwan’s office in his country despite domestic challenges in doing so.

The most important meeting will be between Xi and Trump. The leaders of the world’s two superpowers are expected to tackle a broad range of issues including AI and trade. In a move that could strain the fragile tariff truce that the two leaders first agreed last year, the Trump administration said on Monday it would further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips.

Christopher Adams, a senior adviser at the law firm Covington who was at the centre of trade negotiations with China for the Obama and first Trump administrations, said: “The trade truce may increasingly look like a ceasefire in a war where major combat operations remain on hold but skirmishes are escalating to the point where the line between peace and war is blurred.

“I don’t see pressure to announce a further extension of the trade truce in Shenzhen. If a significant extension is announced, that would be an upside surprise.”

China has not hesitated to leverage Apec’s multinational platform in service of its arguments. A commentary by the state news agency Xinhua on Tuesday said: “Amid deepening geopolitical rivalries and growing global divisions, [China’s hosting] sends a clear signal that great-power competition need not be a zero-sum game, and that one country’s development need not come at the expense of another.”

The chair of the Apec senior officials’ meeting, Chen Xu, said Beijing had made trade “openness” a key focus of its Apec year and looked forward to “achieving more practical outcomes on the trade front”.

The much anticipated trilateral summit with Trump and Putin, on the other hand, could prove largely symbolic. For Xi, “it provides the appearance of China shaping the world order as an equal to the United States,” said Dr Kevork Oskanian, an expert on Russia at the University of Exeter. “Agreement on substantial issues, which would, in any case, require extensive preparatory negotiations, is unlikely.”

For China’s ruling Communist party, the political pomp has another key purpose. Nordin said summits were “occasions for leaders to tell stories about the world, about their country’s place in it … and one of the most important audiences for those stories is at home.”

For the locals watching the skyscraper light show on Monday night, the symbolism was not lost. China’s export might had helped it become increasingly powerful on the world stage, said one local man, who did not give his name. “It’s so great that the summit will take place in Shenzhen,” he said. “I feel very proud.”

stories.title: The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left
stories.summary: Andy Burnham wants "steps" towards a closer EU alignment. But the bloc has changed considerably since the UK left it
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left

Published 6 hours ago

"Opening the door to uncontrolled immigration," is how Reform UK described it. "Dragging us into the European Union via the back door," was the charge levelled by the Conservatives.

You could be forgiven for expecting drastic change come Friday's EU-UK summit in Brussels judging by some of the criticism levelled by opponents of the Labour government.

Instead, what's on the table is a limited youth work and mobility scheme (the source of Reform's ire), agreement on cross-channel carbon emissions pricing and a deal to ease food trade.

There's also talk of reducing tuition fees for EU students at British universities (something EU member states, like Germany, really want) in exchange for the UK being admitted to an EU manufacturing scheme (which is important to the Burnham government).

Even in these limited areas, I'm told, not all details will be ironed out by the time of Friday's meeting.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham admitted last week this is all a "step" towards a closer working relationship with Europe.

It's certainly not a leap, and definitely not a matter of rejoining the bloc at this stage.

Other "steps" under immediate discussion are the UK rejoining the EU's electricity market, and the UK trying again to join an EU-backed defence loan scheme.

"Small steps… to make both sides stronger," is how the EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas describes this process. She also warns: "We have in Europe a lot of trauma from Britain leaving [the EU], so things will not be easy."

At this week's summit, the UK and EU are expected to discuss a limited youth mobility scheme, cross-channel carbon emissions pricing, and a deal to ease food trade

Bigger, potentially more politically explosive EU-UK questions look likely to follow after Friday's summit. It's thought Burnham may propose rejoining the EU's customs union and/or the single market. There are suggestions he could eventually table a new referendum on rejoining the EU. None of this before the next general election, though.

On this side of the Channel, the debate is very much focused on what Britain might want. Burnham's plan is bold, belated or completely barmy - depending on your political perspective. But there's been little discussion about the EU point of view, and less still on how the EU has changed since Britain left it.

Just how different is the EU in 2026 from the bloc Britain turned its back on a decade ago? And with the UK still mired in arguments over its relationship with Europe, does the EU even want GB back in the fold or would Brussels now rather avoid more drama?

A series of shocks

Since 2016, a series of international shocks have fundamentally changed the EU.

The Covid crisis collapsed international supply chains. Europe became aware just how dependent it was on China for medical supplies, for example. Then, Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine showed the EU how utterly reliant many members were on energy supplies from Moscow. Big EU beasts like Germany and Italy were particularly affected.

The Ukraine war, the continent's biggest active conflict since World War Two, has persuaded the EU that Europe's domestic defence industry and industrial policy needs a boost and far better coordination.

Donald Trump's two stints as US president convinced the EU that it can never again fully rely on the US to be Europe's best friend abroad, either in trade or security terms. And China's attempt to 'dump' cheap cars and steel in Europe, hurting the Continent's businesses, has made the EU more protectionist-minded.

Brussels's main takeaways: Europe should become more self-reliant. And where imports are needed - with fossil fuels, for example - it must diversify which countries it buys from.

The French used to be a lone voice amongst big EU countries, pushing for more protectionism. Other member states prioritised finding the lowest possible prices, as was once the case with Russian gas, for example. Now there's a growing acceptance that economic efficiency must at times be sacrificed to achieve security of supply.

Some think the UK won't want to align itself with an increasingly protectionist, borrow-happy bloc. While an EU member, the free-trade-minded UK was credited with pushing Brussels to be more "British" and make its single market more competitive.

Britain's 2016 EU referendum prompted years of political drama

Others point out that Britain has also changed since 2016.

"The British are less 'British' than they once were," Charles Grant, director of the Centre for European Reform, told me. When the EU introduced steel tariffs to protect itself against Chinese dumping, the UK followed suit with its own, similar tariffs. Now, the EU is placing high tariffs on Chinese imports of electric vehicles - and once again the UK is considering a similar move. "Everyone is a bit more French now," says Grant.

Another big EU change, according to European policy expert Georgina Wright, is that EU citizens have become more comfortable with the idea of centralised European power: a pooling of sovereignty in times of emergency.

The Covid crisis prompted the EU to embrace 'common borrowing', where Brussels raises debt on behalf of member states, who then share the benefits and the risks. It was a historic move, particularly for Germany which was once allergic to the idea. Now there's discussion about a new round of common borrowing focused on defence, in answer to Russian aggression and a US proposing to withdraw defence capabilities from Europe.

Some in the EU tell me that none of this would be possible had the more sovereign-minded UK remained a member state.

A changing EU

But there are political winds of change blowing through the bloc.

Nationalist, more Eurosceptic parties are polling strongly in big EU members states ahead of upcoming elections. The EU that Burnham wants Britain to align with might look very different by the end of next year.

In France, one of the EU's two most influential countries, the hard-right leader Marine Le Pen is leading opinion polls ahead of the spring presidential election. Nation-first parties in Italy, Spain and Poland, as in France, say they want to transform the bloc from the inside.

Britain's centre-left government - as well as some UK voters - might be put off by an EU with Le Pen as a dominant force.

Conversely, there's an argument that an EU led by Eurosceptics might actually become more appealing to Britain. While those parties have their differences, they generally want to take powers back from Brussels, making the EU a looser club of stronger nation states - less of a political project, and more of a transactional club of common economic interests.

One change we can pretty much bet on is this: if Le Pen becomes French president, Brussels will become embroiled in internal existential tussles over the EU's future. These fault lines will pit the left against the right; pro-Europeans against Eurosceptics; Ukraine backers against those (like Le Pen) who want to stop financial aid; fans of a bigger EU budget against parties wanting to slash national contributions.

With all that going on, negotiations with the UK would very likely slip further down the priority list. British diplomats might find their calls unanswered.

If Burnham really wants to get closer to the EU, the time to act is now, says Wright. She identifies a window of opportunity before France's election for the UK to get "creative" in its re-set proposals.

Marine Le Pen leads the polls in France for next year's presidential election

Brussels is certainly under pressure to be more flexible in its relations with trusted allies outside the bloc, because of the threatening geopolitical climate. The EU embrace of Canada is a clear example.

"The prime minister should get out and about on the continent more, be more visible and talk more positively about what can be done together," says Wright.

Wright insists people in the UK are open to the idea. She quotes a survey by the National Centre for Social Research, published this month, which suggests 42% of Britons prioritise closer links with Europe over the US, while only 9% of Britons prioritise links with the US.

What Brussels wants

Then there's the question of how much Brussels actually wants Britain back in the European bloc.

Some in the UK believe they could take advantage of current geopolitical uncertainty. With the Russian threat looming, they think Brussels wants to have the UK close because of the UK's military and nuclear capabilities. In exchange, the UK could push for an ambitious deal with the EU, says Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey.

But Dr Ilke Toygür, a politics professor at Madrid's IE University, points out that European countries already work closely with the UK in defence, through Nato and the British and French-led support for Ukraine - so UK military leverage may not matter so much in EU terms.

Having the UK back in the European Union would certainly give the bloc more economic heft. In fact, some in the UK argue Britain is far better outside the bloc. Member states' economies are struggling, they say: look at stagnant Germany and Italy, and spluttering France. The UK, on the other hand, has grown at its fastest rate in two years thanks to AI investment. The UK enjoys freedom to regulate the AI industry outside the EU that it wouldn't have as an EU member state.

But EU diplomats I speak to believe the UK needs Brussels more than the other way round.

Germany and some European countries are investing in defence - and Britain now wants to join an EU-backed defence loan scheme

"The UK alone is a middling power in a field of giants," an EU diplomat from a big European country told me. He asked to remain anonymous in order to speak freely. "With China on the one side and the US on the other, the UK will be trampled underfoot if it stands alone. It must know that."

If the UK were ever to rejoin the EU, he says, it wouldn't necessarily have to join the euro currency or the open-border Schengen scheme.

But Michael Barnier, the former EU lead Brexit negotiator, tells me that as long as Britain remains outside the bloc it can't just cherry-pick all the benefits . It's the same argument the UK faced during cross-channel talks 10 years ago. The EU views the single market as the jewel in the bloc's crown, says Barnier, and Brussels does not want to devalue it by making major exceptions for the UK that other non-EU countries would then demand too. But he adds that the UK remains a much-appreciated ally and trading partner.

It would help Burnham, says the academic Toygür, if the UK had a more positive story to tell. She says Brussels is used to hearing Britain saying "we want to get closer to the EU because it's better for UK economic interests". Instead they should emphasise benefits to the EU, she says.

"We face a competition of great powers (China, US, Russia) and we are stronger together.

"The UK needs to commit resources: innovation and financial capacities to a continental-level project. It doesn't have to call that project 'the EU' but this is the only story moving forward."

What you hear from EU diplomats is that member states are more than OK with the existing post-Brexit trade deal. There is not a huge appetite to unravel it and start again.

The "little steps" of change, beneficial to both sides, like easing exports and imports, are what the EU is comfortable with right now.

Still, economist Heather Grabbe, from the Brussels-based economic think-tank Bruegel, predicts an "inevitable drift together" between the two sides.

British universities have historically been popular with Europeans - and now Brussels wants the UK to lower tuition fees for EU students

"We face the same challenges: aging populations, wildfires and storms, the impact of climate change, with our continent warming at twice the global rate. Russia is attacking us all with its hybrid warfare, we have the same outlook in world affairs: we're not pro-Trump, we're not pro-Putin. Working together makes sense," she says.

EU countries express a lot of warmth when asked about the UK inching closer. But behind closed doors, there is clear reticence. "Commitment" is a word you hear over and again; they're not sure that Britain really means it. They hear the Conservative Party deputy leader, Alex Burghart, for example, who vowed that, if elected, his party would "rip up" Labour's upcoming UK-EU agreements.

"The UK first needs a national conversation. And a binding decision. They need to know what they want and stick to it," say EU figures I speak to.

This is exactly what the EU insisted on 10 years ago, after the UK voted for Brexit without a clear political plan for what future relations with the bloc should look like.

As a journalist who's covered the UK's divorce from the EU right from the outset, I'm getting a rather strong sense of déjà vu.
