stories.title: Government risks missing climate targets if EV rules weakened, adviser warns
stories.summary: The UK could miss legally binding climate targets if EV targets are cut, an adviser warns
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Current rules say all new cars must be zero emission by 2035

Published 6 hours ago

The UK is likely to miss legally binding climate targets if the government reduces electric vehicle (EV) targets, independent adviser the Climate Change Committee (CCC) has warned.

In a letter to Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander, the CCC argues that weakening the targets would result in "economic and energy security costs" and leave households "more exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices".

The CCC says that switching to an electric vehicle can save a typical household around £800 a year, with fewer people benefiting if the targets were watered down.

The warning comes after weeks of speculation that the government plans to announce changes to the EV targets. Government sources insist no decision has been made.

Under the current rules, a "zero emission vehicle" (ZEV) mandate requires 80% of new cars sold in the UK to be zero emission by 2030 and all new cars to meet that standard by 2035. Companies that fail to meet their ZEV mandate face a potential fine of £12,000 per car, although there are exemptions.

Industry groups have long complained the current rules impose too heavy a burden, calling instead for a "sustainable transition".

Latest data from trade body the Society of Motor Manufacturing and Traders (SMMT) shows that EVs, as well as plug-in hybrids, are driving growth in new car sales.

In the year so far, 26.6% of all new car registrations have been fully electric, the SMMT says, which is below the headline target of 33% for 2026.

But the industry as a whole appears on course to comply with this year's mandate once flexibilities are accounted for, according to analysis by New AutoMotive, a transport research organisation which supports the transition to electric cars

SMMT Chief Executive Mike Hawes accused the CCC of ignoring the costs of the targets it was defending.

"The industry cannot subsidise the transition indefinitely, which is why it is unified in seeking change," he said.

Carbon budget

The CCC analysis also argued that weakening the targets would lead to a hole in the government's carbon savings that need to be made in order to meet its legally binding climate targets.

The CCC said the ZEV mandate "underpins the largest share of emissions reduction to 2037" in the government's net-zero plan. The climate targets set for 2033-2037 will be missed "without alternative action at the same scale", the CCC argued.

CCC analysis shows surface transport - which includes cars, vans and trucks - remains the country's highest carbon-emitting sector and one of the slowest to decarbonise.

Lord Deben, former CCC chairman, said going against CCC advice would "not be sensible" as it would "cost people money".

He said climate targets were "not random targets" and "if you don't reach them then you put yourselves in really serious danger of having climate change, which we can't handle".

A government spokesperson said: "We remain committed to the phase out of all new petrol and diesel cars by 2030 and to all new car and van sales being zero emission by 2035, as well as to our legally binding net zero targets. Our consultation on the Mandate will not change this and will ensure we are taking a pragmatic and balanced approach to the ZEV transition."

stories.title: Burnham to set out options next month for long-term EU relationship
stories.summary: The prime minister says he will set out options for the future "alongside" his 10-year economic plan.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 17 November 2026

Andy Burnham has said he plans to set out his proposed options to reshape the UK's future relationship with the EU next month.

Downing Street had been facing pressure to specify when the prime minister would take this step, after he previously said he would do so "around" a summit taking place in Brussels this week.

Burnham will travel to the meeting with the EU this Friday, where both sides hope to unveil new agreements on food, youth visas and re-linking British industry to the EU's carbon trading regime.

However, it is understood he will not indicate any preference at this stage which of the long-term options he could back in future.

Former Prime Minister Boris Johnson said Burnham would be wasting his premiership by reopening arguments about Brexit.

Speaking to Sky News, Burnham said: "I'm in a negotiation about improving the Brexit deal - that's what I'm doing this week. We'll see how it goes.

"And then we will consider whether there are options to further the relationship with the EU."

He added this would be set out "alongside" the 10-year plan for the economy that he has promised to unveil before Parliament breaks for Christmas.

Burnham has previously suggested he could commit Labour to pursuing a much closer future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member, though he has ruled out major changes before the next election.

The party's 2024 manifesto promised not to return to the EU single market, customs union or freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa.

Negotiations for the deals to be unveiled on Friday began under Burnham's predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, but Burnham has indicated he believes the UK's Brexit deal needs to be revised further.

Making his first major foreign policy speech on Monday night, Burnham told his audience: "After the summit, we will initiate a discussion with our EU partners about options for our long-term relationship.

"This will take time, and we will present those options and our assessment of them to inform decisions in the next Parliament."

In September, Burnham told the Labour Party conference he would "take the opportunity around the summit to lay out to you, to lay out to the country, what I believe are the different options for Britain's long-term relationship with our European partners".

Asked on Tuesday whether Burnham was now "hitting the brakes" and pushing any announcement of options back further into the future, a No 10 spokesman said earlier: "I don't accept that characterisation."

And speaking to Sky News, Burnham rejected the idea he was stepping back, arguing he was "doing exactly what I said".

"I will set out next month what the next phase looks like, and that is exactly what I said at my conference speech."

Former Foreign Secretary David Lammy has said Labour should go into the next election promising to rejoin the EU.

Writing in The Times on Tuesday, , external he said the prime minister's conference speech in Liverpool "didn't only ignite a debate around joining the EU - it blew the door wide open".

"Burnham is right to break glass on the European question because membership is the greatest growth accelerator the government has available."

'Madness'

He also dismissed Johnson's warning against reopening arguments about Brexit.

Johnson had told the Daily Telegraph , external : "It is madness to escalate the Brexit issue as your political priority.

"He will impale himself and his party on this point, and he needs to move off it because he won't win – because the reality is that people are not fools."

Responding to his comments, Burnham said: "I just don't think he's an authority on these matters.

"I'm afraid I'm not going to listen to Boris Johnson on this particular matter. He burned bridges and created a lot of bad feeling, and consequently, Britain suffered as a result of that."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage MP said Burnham was "turning his back" on his constituents in Makerfield, where two-thirds of residents voted for Brexit in the 2016 referendum.

"We haven't taken the full advantage of Brexit and the idea of tying us back to single market rules overseen by the [European Court of Justice] is nothing less than a democratic outrage," he added.

stories.title: Home secretary plans to tackle 'perception of two-tier policing'
stories.summary: Shabana Mahmood will announce stronger guidance on police impartiality.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 8 hours ago

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood is to announce stronger guidance on police impartiality to tackle what she calls the "corrosive and growing perception of two-tier policing".

She will tell a conference of police chiefs that they should avoid what she calls "misguided attempts at course correction" where the pursuit of equality leads instead to differential treatment.

Recent complaints about alleged two-tier policing have mostly come from those on the right in politics.

They have pointed to the arrest of Henry Nowak as he was dying after being stabbed by Vickrum Digwa who had accused him of racism.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has argued that white people are treated differently by police because of their race. But critics say this claim risks overlooking the long‑standing experiences of black and minority ethnic communities.

Some senior police figures have also strongly rejected the claim of two-tier policing.

Mahmood will announce a new national standard is being developed "to ensure all members of the public are treated equally", said the Home Office.

"Now let me be clear: I know the vast majority of officers police impartially and that policing without fear or favour is their creed," she will say.

But Mahmood will announce "clear, comprehensive guidance" on police impartiality, which reinforces that officers must apply the law consistently to avoid what she called "motivated actors" whipping up the idea that there's two-tier policing.

Mahmood will say that community engagement can mean going to a residents' association meeting and having tea and biscuits - or samosas - but it shouldn't mean engaging with activists pushing an agenda.

"Leave the politics to the politicians," she will say. "And we will leave the policing to you."

The home secretary will add that more needs to be done to tackle inequalities in policing, highlighting the persistently low proportion of black police officers.

However, she will state that some "well-intentioned approaches", such as the Police Anti-Racism Commitment, "have risked undermining confidence in impartial policing".

"As a Muslim home secretary, no one can doubt that equality in policing, and in our forces, matters to me," she will say.

"But we must also be wary of misguided attempts at course correction, where the pursuit of equality leads instead to differential treatment.

"To the public, it was patently absurd to tell police officers that fair policing "does not mean treating everyone the same."

Jo Noakes who leads the College of Policing, the standards-setting body for the police, said it will issue new guidance for officers that will make clear on impartiality in Spring.

She said: "Policing must act in a way that maintains public confidence, which is dependent on officers and staff exercising their powers without fear or favour...

"Impartiality cannot be seen in isolation but needs to be considered alongside how policing acts with fairness and inclusion - both in its own ranks and with the public."

stories.title: Former Conservative MP Sir David Evennett dies
stories.summary: Sir David Evennett was a Conservative MP in south-east London for more than 30 years.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Sir David Evennett was a London MP for more than 30 years

Published 17 November 2026

Sir David Evennett, who served as a Conservative MP in south-east London for more than 30 years, has died aged 77 after a short illness.

He was first elected as MP for Erith and Crayford in 1983 but lost his seat in 1997. In 2005 he was elected as the MP for Bexleyheath and Crayford, a position he held until he decided not to run in the 2024 general election.

Sir David served as a Tory whip in opposition and in government, and was a vice-chairman of the party. He started his career as a teacher, and then became a councillor for Redbridge in east London.

Conservative Party chairman Kevin Hollinrake said Sir David was a "diligent" MP and "true champion of Conservatism".

Hollinrake added: "Even once he left the House of Commons, he was still a regular attendee at Kemi's (Kemi Badenoch's) speeches and an assiduous local campaigner.

"May he rest in peace."

Sir David also worked as a marine insurance broker at Lloyds and a lecturer in management for Bexley College.

He is survived by his wife Marilyn and his two sons.

stories.title: Ex-Reform Wales leader Dan Thomas faces no further police action after assault arrest
stories.summary: Gwent Police says Reform MS faces no further action for arrest that led to him standing down as leader.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Dan Thomas, who resigned from his role as Reform's leader in Wales, says he's been "vindicated"

Published 17 November 2026

A police investigation into Reform's former leader in Wales has been dropped, two months after he was arrested on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour.

Thomas said he had been "vindicated" by Gwent Police's decision that he should face no further action.

The arrest had led the Member of Senedd (MS) for Casnewydd Islwyn to resign from his role leading the largest Senedd opposition group , triggering a leadership contest and the election of Helen Jenner as his replacement .

Nigel Farage said he was "very pleased that Dan Thomas has been cleared", adding he had "stood by him throughout this process".

Jenner will remain as the party's Welsh leader, the BBC understands.

Thomas said he had been subjected to "false allegations" and had been "fully cooperating with the police".

"When this began, I said I had done nothing wrong. Today, I have been vindicated."

He said Farage, Jenner and Senedd colleagues had been "incredibly supportive".

"To my family and the people of Blackwood, my hometown, thank you for standing by me. Those constituents who have stopped me in the street to wish me well have been a real source of strength."

On X, Jenner said it was "great news".

She added she was "so pleased to see a close friend having his name cleared".

Dan Thomas was picked by Farage to be the party's Welsh leader before the 2026 Senedd election.

The news that he was quitting as leader following the arrest broke on the same day that Sarah Cooper-Lessad announced that she was quitting his party for Plaid Cymru.

At the time of the arrest Gwent Police said a 45-year-old man from Aberbargoed, Caerphilly, had been arrested on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour.

A spokesperson for Gwent Police said: "We take all allegations of assault and controlling and coercive behaviour extremely seriously, [and] a thorough investigation took place.

"The 45-year-old man who was arrested has been released with no further action."

stories.title: We can't afford to hire under-25s, say firms. Will Milburn plans help?
stories.summary: The proposal to cut employers' National Insurance costs is "essential" to tackling the Neet problem, one business group says.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 17 November 2026

Lowering employers' National Insurance (NI) payments for those between 21 and 24, and cash incentives to take on some workers are among proposals put forward in Alan Milburn's report to get more 18-24 year-olds working.

Many companies have complained that recent increases in National Insurance and the minimum wage have made it more expensive to take on staff.

We talked to firms and business groups about the issues they face when hiring younger workers and what they make of the proposals.

Costs the key issue

Bournemouth-based café owner Ben Blades says he cannot justify the extra cost of training up new staff

Cutting NI costs is "right in the sweet spot of what firms need to hit the hire button", said the Recruitment and Employment Confederation (REC).

The Milburn report proposes NI thresholds could be raised over the next five years, from £5,000 to £10,000 for those aged 21 to 24, and suggests prioritising the retail and hospitality sectors.

Bournemouth-based café owner Ben Blades says the high costs he faces currently make it difficult to employ young people with no work experience.

"My labour costs are already over 45%. We simply cannot justify the extra cost to put on an extra staff member to train someone up for three months," he says.

"In hospitality our margins have been squeezed and squeezed and squeezed"

As a result, he says it currently makes more sense to employ someone who already has experience.

Major report proposes welfare changes, apprenticeships and tax cuts to help 440,000 young people into work

At a glance: Key proposals from Milburn's Neets report Published 19 hours ago

Allen Simpson, chief executive of UKHospitality, says the recommendation to raise the threshold is "the right one" and "would be an immediate shot in the arm for job creation".

But the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) argues the Milburn report does not go far enough in tackling costs facing businesses.

It says while the NI proposal is welcome, the change should be wider than just retail and hospitality, otherwise it "risks adding complexity and blocking off potential career paths".

Cash incentives

Ally Fir says if a state scheme was running she'd "jump on it right away"

Other proposals put forward by the Milburn review include cash incentives to employ younger workers.

Employers who take on any young person who has been Neet - not in education, employment or training - for six months should receive a £3,000 payment, and small businesses - with less than 50 employees - that do so should receive an extra £2,000

There would also be an extra £2,000 payment if the young person has been in care or is disabled.

Ally Fir runs a bookshop in Westbourne, alongside her partner Matt, and thinks more state support is needed.

She says incentivised schemes for small business "would help us to employ more, especially young people. If a scheme like that was going we'd jump on it right away."

Fir says she gets job applications "every single day". She'd like to take more people on but "it is the cost of employing people that makes that impossible".

Tom Parsons has already had experience of using government schemes to employ young people at his design consultancy, Aetha, in Poole, Dorset.

The Kickstart Scheme in 2020 meant he could take on two young people in fully funded six-month job placements offering 25 hours a week.

Tom Parsons says the old Kickstart Scheme was a game-changer for those employed under it

"One of them stayed with us for five years and the other one I think about three years. And it completely changed the game for them," Tom told the BBC. "So if there was a scheme like that, again, that would really help us."

He says he wants to employ young people but costs remain a huge barrier.

Where are the most jobs for 18-24 year-olds? Published 18 hours ago

Why Milburn's Neets reforms will only save £200m a year by 2036 Published 18 hours ago

Guaranteed hours a concern

One of the government's flagship employment rights reforms risks weakening the hiring of young people, according to Milburn's report.

Ministers are abolishing what they call ''exploitative'' zero-hours contracts and replacing them with guaranteed hours contracts which would be based on the number of hours people normally work.

Much of the detail is yet to be finalised but the Employment Rights Act is due to be enacted next year.

Milburn is concerned that the changes could cause problems "at a time when the youth labour market is already weak'.'

The REC said companies were "particularly worried" over the guaranteed hours measure.

It added that addressing the Neets problem gave ministers "the perfect opportunity" to reconsider the issue.

Help getting staff

Young people should have a legal right to a route into education, training or work, and would be supported to do so under an "opportunity guarantee", Milburn has proposed.

This could help firms which are struggling to recruit. Thirty-five-year-old Dean Greene, a sales director at waste management facility Williams Environmental, says it's tricky finding staff.

"We didn't get many applicants for it at all," says Greene, referencing an ad for a marketing and sales role.

"There wasn't a huge uptake from that sort of 16-to-24 range," he adds.

He thinks the lack of applicants may be because the waste industry is perceived as "mucky and dirty", but he is confident many would be interested if they knew the job was available.

Pointing to himself as an example of progressing in the industry, he tells me how he started as an admin officer scanning paperwork at 18 before remaining with the company for 17 years.

stories.title: Why Milburn's Neets reforms will only save £200m a year by 2036
stories.summary: Milburn's plan to help young people promises to save money from the UK's welfare bill. BBC Verify has taken a look at the numbers.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 17 November 2026

Alan Milburn's long-awaited plan to help young people who are neither learning nor earning promises to save money from the UK's welfare bill.

Milburn said he believes his proposed reforms, which would reduce benefits for some young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neets) but aim to get them jobs in the long run, could save as much as £13.8bn in welfare costs over the next 10 years.

But after the extra spending he has proposed for job guarantees from the government, hiring incentives for firms, and health and education support, his reforms are only projected to save £200m a year of taxpayers' money overall by 2036.

BBC Verify has taken a look through the numbers.

Burnham wants Neets report to be watershed moment, No 10 says, as Tories criticise welfare and tax proposals

How many young people claim benefits?

Analysts have expressed concerns about the sharply rising number of young people claiming health and disability benefits in recent years.

The Milburn report estimates that around £8bn a year is currently being spent on benefits directly for young people through the welfare system, made up of £4.6bn on Universal Credit and £3.2bn on Personal independence payments (Pip).

The number of 16-24 year olds in England and Wales claiming the health element of Universal Credit has increased from 105,000 in 2020 to 193,000 this year according to the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP).

Young Pip claimants have also increased from 230,000 to 511,000 over that time, while official forecasts suggest this number is set to rise , external above 800,000 by 2037.

The young people caught up in Britain's Neets crisis Published 19 hours ago

Would Milburn's reforms reduce welfare spending?

Milburn's reforms would combine two major policies in relation to young people:

A significant increase in government spending to help them into employment and training

Reductions in the welfare payments available to some of the group

Milburn's long-term plans call for an additional £5.8bn in spending per year by 2036 on things such as employment subsidies and mental health support to help get young people into work or education.

He is also proposing a new benefits system so young people would not be able to access the same kind of health and disability benefits as older people, including creating a Youth Allowance instead of giving under-25s Universal Credit and a new Additional Cost Allowance that could replace Pip benefits.

Milburn estimates that these reforms would contribute to a reduction of total welfare spending of £3.6bn a year by 2036 relative to where spending would otherwise have been in that year, and said it could save a cumulative £13.8bn from the welfare bill over the next decade.

Milburn said his diagnosis applies UK-wide, but education, skills, health and local government are devolved to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. He has called on the devolved administrations to agree "a shared set of headline outcomes".

At a glance: Key proposals from Milburn's Neets report Published 19 hours ago

Where are the most jobs for 18-24 year-olds? Published 18 hours ago

Watch: What's in the Milburn review? Published 19 hours ago

How big is the total welfare bill?

Official forecasts show the total welfare system , external is projected to cost £353bn this year. There is no official forecast of the level of total welfare spending in 2036, but likely inflation means it would be above the £431bn currently projected for 2032.

Around half of this cost is the state pension, on which spending is forecast to rise from £154bn a year to £193bn a year. Spending on Pip and disability living allowance are also set to rise over that time from £40bn a year to £57bn a year.

However, as a share of the overall economy, the increase in the cost of the welfare system is less dramatic.

Total welfare spending is forecast to rise from 11.1% of GDP this year to 11.3% in 2032. This would be below the the peak of around 12% seen in 2013 following the global financial crisis.

That has led some economists and researchers to question the argument , external that welfare spending is out of control.

The reductions touted as part of Milburn's reforms, if delivered, is likely to only reduce the UK's benefits bill by a relatively small amount.

As a share of today's welfare bill, the £3.6bn of annual savings in 2036 would be only 1%.

How much could the reforms save?

As well as the £5.8bn that would be spent on supporting young people into work, training or college, Milburn estimates the government would reap £2.4bn a year in additional taxes, as more people would be in work.

This £2.4bn of additional taxes combined with the £3.6bn in lower welfare spending would add up to £6bn a year in 2036.

That implies a net saving for the government as a result of Milburn's proposed package of £200m by that year, although this saving would grow over time.

The £200m net savings figure in the Milburn report is also in today's money - and would be larger in cash terms in 2036, though the actual cash figure will depend on inflation over the next decade.

stories.title: What does Neet stand for and why does the UK have so many?
stories.summary: Ministers want to tackle the high number of young people not in education, employment or training.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 19 November 2025

A major review by former minister Alan Milburn has suggested widespread reforms to get young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neet) into work across the UK.

His review , external says the UK should aim to reduce the rate of Neet young people from 13% to about 5% by 2036.

The recommendations relate mostly to England, but Milburn has said many can be adapted to the devolved systems in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland too.

What does Neet mean?

A young person is considered Neet if they are n ot in e ducation, e mployment or t raining.

To be considered Neet, a person must be aged 16 to 24 and:

unemployed - looking for work

economically inactive - not actively looking for work and not waiting to start a job, or caring for family

not in formal education, such as school or university, or on a vocational course

not participating in any training schemes, such as apprenticeships or internships

At a glance: Key proposals from Milburn's Neets report Published 19 hours ago

How many Neets are there?

There were 981,000 Neets between April and June, the ONS says, an increase of about 3% on the same period in 2025.

The numbers are published every three months and vary throughout the year, but have been steadily increasing over time.

The latest figures account for 13% - over one in eight - of all young people in the UK.

There were more Neets classed as not looking or available for work than there were hunting for jobs.

The number of economically inactive young people was 588,000. This group includes 310,000 women and 278,000 men.

The ONS estimates that 393,000 16- to 24-year-olds were unemployed and looking for work. There were more unemployed young men than young women - 252,000 men compared with 141,000 women.

An estimated one in 10 young people who are Neet are graduates. However, those who have not achieved GCSE-level qualification are more likely to remain Neet for longer periods, according to the Youth Futures Foundation, an organisation which aims to ensure young people can find work.

It said those living in poverty, or with special educational needs, are also more likely to be Neet.

The ONS releases figures on the number of Neets in the UK every three months.

It produces its estimates from its Labour Force Survey. Fewer people have responded to the survey in recent years, which makes the results more volatile than in the past. The number of Neets tends to fluctuate throughout the year.

Why are there so many Neets and what is the impact?

Tens of thousands of jobs have been lost from the hospitality sector, which tends to employ a significant proportion of young people

Milburn's review challenged the idea that young people were not trying to find work, or were "work-shy, snowflakes, soft".

A survey carried out for his interim report suggested that 84% of Neet young people do want a job or training.

He said rejections for young jobseekers, after submitting dozens, sometimes hundreds of applications, had become the norm.

The report said there was not one factor causing the crisis, with a "perfect storm" of the jobs market, spending on education and the Covid pandemic being some of the reasons highlighted.

It said the number of entry-level jobs had fallen by about 1.6 million over the past 20 years. Vacancies in hospitality, for example, have halved in the last four years alone. Apprenticeships and graduate jobs have also been affected.

Want your job application to stand out? Employers say they look for these six skills Published 27 August

Health issues are also a factor. The proportion of people who say they are Neet because of a work-limiting health condition has increased by 70% over the past decade, according to the Health Foundation charity.

The proportion of Neets citing a mental health condition has more than doubled since 2012 to one in five, according to the most recent Labour Force Survey , external .

Milburn described the situation for young people with disabilities as "devastating". In 2024-2025, 29.6% of disabled young people were Neet, compared with 8.7% of their non-disabled peers, his report said.

What is the government doing about Neets?

Prime Minister Andy Burnham visited a train maunfacturing site in Derby as he set out his plans for technical education

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden welcomed Milburn's report and said the government was already taking action.

He said the government's job guarantee was supporting those "most in need", with the first young people who were supported by the scheme now in work.

"Our wider £2.5bn investment will help create almost a million opportunities to earn or learn," he said, adding that further reforms would follow the review.

However, shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately criticised the government's policies, claiming Labour had "destroyed job opportunities for young people" through increased taxes, such as employer National Insurance contributions .

Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson Daisy Cooper said her party "repeatedly warned that Labour's jobs tax would hammer job opportunities for young people and that their business rates hikes would kill off high street job opportunities".

Minister backs legal right to job support for young people Published 2 days ago

What else is being done across the UK?

In Wales , the Young Person's Guarantee , external was introduced in 2021 to help 16- to 24-year-olds choose the right course, find an apprenticeship, search for jobs or start a business.

In Scotland , the Developing the Young Workforce (DYW) scheme , external was announced in the wake of the Covid pandemic to connect young people with appropriate opportunities such as apprenticeships, work experience or formal volunteering.

In Northern Ireland , there are a range of schemes aimed at helping Neets.

How do other countries help young people find work?

In his interim report, Milburn said the number of young people out of work, training or education in the UK is three times higher than in the Netherlands and twice as high as in Ireland.

A 2025 report from the Youth Futures Foundation , external said the Neet rate in the Netherlands has been steadily under 5% in the last decade.

It said the Netherlands has implemented significant reforms to support youth unemployment over the past two decades, including employment incentives like wage subsidies.

Interventions at national and regional levels include financial support, tailored career guidance, vocational training and structural reforms.

Career guidance in the Netherlands is mandatory in secondary school, and includes information on vocational education, the report said.

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Beijing stops short of confirming specific agenda, but Trump says denuclearisation, Iran war, trade and Ukraine will be among topics

The meeting of Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen this week will cover topics of “groundbreaking significance” including “safeguarding world peace”, the Chinese foreign ministry has said.

The confirmation of Thursday’s trilateral talks, the first of their kind, will take place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit and cement Xi’s status as a global power broker as he presides over events in the glittering southern tech hub of Shenzhen.

At the White House, Trump told reporters he would be speaking to his Chinese and Russian counterparts about denuclearisation, the war in Iran, economics, trade and “my favourite subject, Ukraine”. US officials had earlier indicated that Trump would not discuss Russia’s war in Ukraine during the trip.

Trump also said he may meet North Korea’s Kim Jong-un in what would be their first meeting of his second term. “We may meet with Kim Jong-un also,” Trump said. “So that will be good … we have a chance to accomplish a lot.”

Asked whether Kim would be there, Trump said that he “may come”. “I don’t know,” he said. “That’s up to president Xi.”

Many, including the UN secretary general, António Guterres, had hoped the trilateral talks would be used to discuss reductions in nuclear arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers.

In a call this week, China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, “agreed on the importance of meaningful leader-level conversations to advance goals such as peace and denuclearisation”, the US state department said.

China was the last of the three powers to confirm the trilateral meeting was happening, and its statement stopped short of confirming specific agenda items.

“[The leaders] will exchange views in-depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance,” said its foreign ministry spokesperson, Mao Ning. “Stronger communication among China, Russia and the United States, along ​with managing differences and stabilising relations, serves the interests of all three countries.”

The Kremlin said: “The significance and symbolism of this meeting are hard to overestimate.”

Separately, the Kremlin ‌spokesperson Dmitry Peskov reportedly said on Monday that Putin would meet Kim, too, ​were he to be invited. “Of course, if ‌he is at the APEC ​summit,” Interfax quoted Peskov as saying. Peskov made ⁠his comments as ​Putin met ​a ​delegation in ​the Kremlin ‌from North ​Korea’s ​ruling Workers party.

Guterres said that if the three leaders “really commit themselves to a meaningful denuclearisation, it will be a great achievement for the world”. However, many analysts have warned to temper expectations of a major breakthrough.

Xi will “bask in the glow of China serving as the convener and agenda-setter”, wrote Brookings’ Ryan Hass in one such take. However, “symbolism may prove more enduring than the substance of this meeting”.

The three leaders would be approaching the talks with very different priorities, Xiaoyu Pu from the University of Nevada told the Guardian.

after newsletter promotion

China has rebuffed previous attempts to become embroiled in nuclear arms talks with ​Russia and the US, which ‌have the larger stockpiles. Trump, though, has said he wants to talk about denuclearisation, as well as the US-Israeli war in Iran. China, a top economic partner of Tehran, has sought to mediate in the conflict and says avoiding a return to hostilities is a “top priority”.

Trump’s remarks that he wanted to discuss Ukraine could stoke fears voiced by the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, that the trilateral talks could turn into a “Yalta 2, 3, 4 with a redistribution of influence”. Zelenskyy was referring to the 1945 pact between the US, UK and Soviet Union that created spheres of influence in Europe after the second world war.

“Ukraine-Russia is losing 25,000 soldiers a month, so we’ll be talking about that,” Trump said. He also deflected criticism of Putin in his remarks, saying the Kremlin leader could be “a lot tougher” in Ukraine and that he was already “backing down”.

US officials had said Trump was not expected to raise the issue, and the German president, Frank-Walter Steinmeier, said Xi showed “irritation” in a recent meeting when the idea of the trilateral talks covering Ukraine came up.

For Xi, much of the political benefit will be simply in “the ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table”, Peter Alexander, the Shanghai-based managing director at Z-Ben Advisors, told CNBC .

The Wall Street Journal reported last week that the Trump administration had pushed back against Beijing’s demands that the summit be tightly scripted, with prepared statements and not much room for discussion.

Sari Arho Havrén, of the Royal United Services Institute thinktank, wrote on X : “China dislikes surprises and wants to ensure neither Trump nor Putin steals the limelight from the host. Moreover, Xi doesn’t want to be dragged into a discussion about Ukraine or anything else he is not prepared for.”

stories.title: Government must act now or lose Royal Mail, former minister warns
stories.summary: The former business secretary says "undercutting" by rivals will make Royal Mail "unviable".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 17 November 2026

Former Business Secretary Peter Kyle has said the government must act urgently to "level the playing field" for Royal Mail or risk the business becoming unviable.

He said he was concerned that the firm was being "undercut" by rival parcel delivery firms who did not employ staff under the same conditions.

Royal Mail, which is owned by International Distribution Services, has struggled in recent years with increased competition, fewer letters being sent and fines from the regulator for missing delivery targets.

A government spokesperson said it would consider whether further reforms are required to the parcel market after the watchdog, Ofcom, publishes its annual monitoring report in December.

Kyle had started to prepare officials at the Department for Business and Trade (DBT) to look at the delivery market for parcels shortly before he was replaced in his job by Jonathan Reynolds as business secretary in July.

He said a "crunch point" had been reached where the government had to make a decision about whether it wants Royal Mail "to be a viable proposition in the future".

He said his review would have looked at where the costs in that market lay and where the profit was being made, to see successful companies upheld "the values of business in Britain today".

"If we leave it another few years then Royal Mail will just become unviable and it will just collapse under the weight of having full-time employees," he said.

According to Royal Mail, 98% of its 130,000 workers are permanent employees, with rights to benefits including pensions, sick pay and holiday pay.

Some other parcel delivery companies use self-employed delivery drivers, with some offering an opt-in service that gives couriers limited additional benefits.

Royal Mail is also legally obliged to offer customers a "one price goes anywhere" service across the UK and to deliver first class letters six days a week to every address.

Kyle's proposed review would not have considered further changes to Royal Mail's universal service obligations or to terms and conditions for its staff.

Former Business Secretary Peter Kyle had planned to launch a review of the parcel delivery market

Royal Mail's performance has improved in recent months but it is still missing its targets for delivering first and second class post.

The firm was fined £21m in October 2025 for missing delivery targets in 2024/25.

Ofcom agreed last year to scrap second class deliveries on Saturdays and to reduce the target for delivering first class post within a day of collection to 90%.

A government spokesperson said the current business secretary had met Royal Mail and the Communication Workers Union, which represents postal workers, last week "to seek timely progress on improving their quality of service and to reiterate our commitment to the company's success."

DBT has also launched a consultation on tackling , external what it calls "bogus" self-employment, which it describes as "a practice whereby some businesses mislabel staff as self-employed to avoid statutory obligations".

Royal Mail has welcomed the consultation, and a spokesperson for the company claimed some parts of the delivery industry were "driving a race to the bottom" on employment standards and said it would "continue to push for a level playing field, with strong and enforceable standards across the industry."

Royal Mail misses delivery targets again but hails 'encouraging' signs Published 21 August

Hundreds of Royal Mail staff quitting each week under new efficiency plans Published 14 October

Many MPs across the UK have reported receiving high volumes of complaints from constituents about missed and delayed deliveries.

Shadow business minister Bradley Thomas said that Royal Mail's management needed to address the business's failings.

"Customers are being asked time and time again to pay increased prices, yet the service they're receiving is not improving," he said.

"Be in no doubt, this is not the fault of the hardworking postmen and women, it's the fault of Royal Mail's management.

"Nationalisation isn't the solution to this problem. Instead, we need ministers and Ofcom to bear down on Royal Mail's management to ensure they deliver on the improvements they've promised their customers."

The Communication Workers Union, which represents Royal Mail workers, is also putting pressure on ministers, with General Secretary Dave Ward calling for a "new model of ownership".

stories.title: The young people caught up in Britain's Neets crisis
stories.summary: BBC News speaks to four of the million young people aged 16 to 24 who are not in work, education or training.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 17 November 2026

The number of young people who are not in work, at school or in college is both an economic and moral crisis, a landmark report into the problem says.

The 241-page report, by ex-Labour minister Alan Milburn, has set out a raft of recommendations for the government to consider.

Ahead of its publication, four young people who are not in education, employment or training - those dubbed as "Neets" - told us why they can't get a job and how the government could help them get one.

Major report proposes welfare changes, apprenticeships and tax cuts to help 440,000 young people into work

Michael: 'Everything is experience, experience, experience'

We meet Michael after his early work experience shift at a supermarket

Michael, 19, who lives with his dad in the Wirral, says he dropped out of college and spent a year at home after his social anxiety "got really bad". It is "very easy" to fall out of the system, he says, if there is little support available.

Michael's story is not unique. There has been a large rise in anxiety and mental health problems in young people .

About one in five Neets have a mental health condition, according to 2025 data , external from the Department for Education (DfE) - more than double the rate in 2012.

Having signed up for Universal Credit, Michael was put in touch with the Merseyside Youth Association to help him find a job. He says mentors there have helped him improve his mental health, which led to him dropping out of college during his A-levels. He says that left him trapped inside his bedroom.

He says jobs in his area are scarce and those that do come up tend to go to older people with more experience. Michael says he is trapped in the cycle of not having the experience needed to build more.

"Everything is experience, experience, experience - that's the one thing that I always used to hear when going for jobs on my own without the help," he says.

We followed Michael for a day, meeting him after his 05:00 start for a work experience shift at a local supermarket that the Merseyside Youth Association helped him get.

Michael says getting his dog Dave motivated him to get out of the house and speak to people more

Lots of Neets receive Universal Credit. For under-25s, the standard rate is £338.58 a month , external , which Michael gets. For some people who cannot work because of a health condition, disability or long-term illness, an additional £217.26 to £429.80 per month may be available.

Ahead of the publication of his full review, it was reported that Milburn would recommend young people should no longer be able to claim those additional health-related benefits, as part of a major overhaul of the welfare system .

Michael acknowledges some young people may be "taking advantage" of the benefits system, but says most "just want the money to get by so they can get a job".

More recently, he has been doing shifts at the Merseyside Youth Centre's on-site cafe to gain more much-needed experience. His hope is to be in a steady job earning money this time next year, with space to have his own art studio one day.

"From three months ago I'm a different person," he says. "I can do stuff, keep going."

At a glance: Key proposals from Milburn's Neets report Published 19 hours ago

Where are the most jobs for 18-24 year-olds? Published 18 hours ago

Watch: What's in the Milburn review? Published 19 hours ago

Maariyah: 'I send 20 job applications a week'

University graduate Maariyah says she is getting turned away from voluntary opportunities

Maariyah, a 22-year-old history and politics graduate, finished her university course last summer. Her dream is to work in museums.

However, she is currently unemployed and looking for any paid job after working a temporary six-month contract for a housing association earlier this year.

She says she spends hours each day in her local library - where she feels more able to focus than she can at home - submitting at least 20 tailored job applications a week.

Those who have not achieved GCSE-level qualifications are more likely to remain Neet for longer periods - however, an estimated one in 10 Neets are university graduates .

Maariyah says she is applying for roles in retail and restaurants, alongside unpaid work experience opportunities in the heritage sector.

But she says she has also been rejected for voluntary roles because they had too many applicants, or because she does not have enough experience. "I'm actively going out of my way to do unpaid work, only to get rejected from these positions," she says.

Not hearing back from employers "happens so often now that's it's like second nature", she says, adding that she finds it frustrating that many of her applications are likely to be screened by AI before a real person sees them.

Maariyah says she tailors her CV and cover letter for over 20 job applications a week

On the day we meet, Maariyah heads to the job centre for her Universal Credit appointment after a library job application session. She says she has noticed an improvement in the support she gets there since she first received the benefit in 2025.

This time, she will be getting some mandatory hospitality training, which she says she is "really glad" to have.

She feels there is a growing sense of disillusionment among others her age. Being on benefits has become normalised because it is so hard to find a job, she adds.

It makes her feel that going to a good university, getting certain grades and doing extracurricular activities "doesn't make a difference in the end".

"I would like employers to give young people a chance to gain experience and take a chance on hard-working people who at the end of the day want a job so that they can contribute to our economy and contribute to their own lives."

Why Milburn's Neets reforms will only save £200m a year by 2036 Published 18 hours ago

Matthieu: 'You might be surprised what people can do'

Matthieu has had many voluntary opportunities, but wants to find paid work

Matthieu, 19, from Edgware in north-west London, is autistic and currently volunteers at a gardening club and a computer repair shop.

We meet him in Finsbury Park, where he is helping to mulch some newly planted trees. Working in nature is calming, he says.

He is looking for work with the support of the charity Ambitious About Autism and his mentor, Annie. He previously did a year-long supported internship with the Whittington hospital.

Matthieu says speaking to people face-to-face there helped his confidence and he enjoyed being part of the team. At his family home, Matthieu's mentor Annie tells us that not having maths and English GCSE qualifications is a barrier to finding employment.

Matthieu says he's more of a manual worker and wants to work in a factory, warehouse or doing deliveries, so that he can contribute financially for his family.

Matthieu enjoys volunteering outside in nature

Those with learning difficulties or autism make up an estimated 12% of Neets, DfE data , external shows. Milburn's interim report , external , which was published in the summer, said 45% of Neets reported having a disability. He said the situation for young disabled people was "devastating".

To make work accessible to him, Matthieu says he would need an employer to take their time with him. He says: "I don't learn that quickly." But he thinks it would be worth it.

"Honestly, you might be surprised what the people can do when you take the time with them and give them that chance," Matthieu says.

Many employers say they can not afford to do so following rises to National Insurance contributions and the minimum wage , which is increasing further as part of announcements made in October's Budget.

Some businesses have told the BBC they are struggling to provide new jobs for young people due to these changes, as well as other factors like rising energy bills.

Although finding work is hard, Matthieu says he remains hopeful because of the support from his internship and job coach.

Alex: 'Places don't want to hire us'

Alex says there aren't many job opportunities in her area

Alex, 20, from St Helens, has been looking for work for a year. She struggles with anxiety and is looking for roles as a cleaner or in retail. She also shares caring responsibilities for her mum with her other family members.

We meet her at Spear, an employment and mindset coaching programme. Alex says her dream is to work with animals. She says she had been studying Level 3 animal management at college before dropping out last year because of her mental health.

"I was so burnt out," she says. "I was struggling to get out of bed, I couldn't do anything. I was dragging myself to college. I was like, 'No, I need to have a break for a bit and try and figure out what to do after that'."

Building up her resilience is something she now works on with a mentor, as well as job applications.

Alex says she is applying for "anything and everything" and wants to get off benefits. She is also currently receiving Universal Credit, which she says is "all the money that I've got until I get a job and I'm earning more".

Alex and her mentor, Grace, work on her CV during one-to-one sessions

When asked what she thinks about potential benefits cuts for young people out of work, Alex says not being able to access benefits would "make life so much worse".

And she says trying to find work in a place like St Helens is harder, because many businesses in the town centre have either "gone or moved or shut down".

"Lots of people think, 'well, young people just don't want to work,'" she says. "But we do. We so desperately want to work. Places don't want to hire us."

Milburn has already said the system isn't working for everyone, and that serious action is needed to avoid young Neets becoming a "lost generation".

Additional reporting by Branwen Jeffreys and Kate McGough

stories.title: Cass report author tells BBC draft conversion practices bill is not workable
stories.summary: The gender care review author says the bill’s wording risks "serious unintended consequences" for parents and therapists.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Baroness Cass said the current wording of the bill risked "serious unintended consequences"

Published 16 November 2026

The author of the independent review into gender identity services for young people says she does not support the current draft bill banning conversion practices - having previously welcomed it.

Baroness Cass told BBC Radio 4's Today programme while it is "desirable" to ban the practices, "the challenge is that we have not yet as far as I can see got a workable bill".

At a parliamentary committee scrutinising the bill, she also said it risked "serious unintended consequences" for parents of children suffering gender distress, or medical professionals working in that area.

A government spokesperson said they welcomed her comments.

They added they would take all evidence put forward by the committee seriously as they "want to get this ban right". The government has said the bill would protect LGBT people in England and Wales.

Conversion practices are generally described as interventions, treatments or activities designed to change or suppress someone's sexual orientation or gender identity.

This can sometimes happen in religious or family settings and can be very distressing for the person at the centre of it.

There have been long-running campaigns in the UK to outlaw such practices, and in its 2024 manifesto, the Labour party promised to introduce a bill banning them.

When the government introduced its draft legislation , external in June this year, Baroness Cass was quoted in the publicity for it , external .

In it, she said: "I am pleased to see that the government is bringing forward legislation which not only gives a clearer definition of what conversion practices are, compared to previous drafts, but also what they are not."

She went on to say she looked forward to the bill receiving further scrutiny before it became law.

But asked at the Draft Conversion Practices Bill committee if she supported the bill's current form, she said simply "no".

Baroness Cass said the increased "polarisation" used in the debate around gender meant people may use the new law in a way that wasn't intended.

The current wording of the bill requires the victim to suffer "serious harm to the individual's physical or mental health, or serious alarm or distress to the individual which has a substantial adverse effect on their usual day-to-day activities".

But Baroness Cass said she worried this wording left open the possibility of "vexatious" complaints that could put therapists working with young gender-distressed people at risk of prosecution.

"Therapeutic interactions can be distressing and often are because you're discussing quite sensitive issues," she told the Today programme.

"So If a young person comes away feeling upset, distressed, angry, that might be the result of a quite appropriate therapeutic intervention but still could be judged as poor professional practice."

She told the committee that professionals working at the new NHS Gender Dysphoria Clinics were concerned that even complaints processes that didn't result in a prosecution could be damaging.

"The problem is the chilling effect of professionals knowing that they may be open to complaint, and indeed prosecution," she told the Today programme.

Baroness Cass also raised concerns about the possible impact the new law could have on families.

She said that, for instance, if a parent stopped a child's money if they thought they might buy a "breast binder or hormones" that this may also fall within the scope of the bill and result in prosecution.

Asked about her apparent support for the bill when it was first published, Baroness Cass said that she was in favour of the idea but had not had the time to read the details before the press release was to be published, but went ahead and gave the quote anyway.

When she published her report on gender identity services for young people in 2024, she described conversion practices as "abhorrent". She says she still feels no LGBT people should be subjected to conversion practices.

She told the committee she wants "a bill that protects the people it's supposed to protect, but doesn't accidentally entrap those who you don't want to [entrap]".

The bill has received support from several LGBT charities, such as Stonewall, and organisations like the British Association for Counselling and Psychotherapy.

The government said: "We want to get this ban right, which is why we have put this draft bill forward for pre-legislative scrutiny.

"We welcome both Baroness Cass's support for taking action to end abusive conversion practices, and her comments on the need for legislation to avoid adverse consequences.

"We will take all evidence put forward by the committee seriously as we move forward in ending almost a decade of delay for LGBT+ people who should never have to suffer abuse in an effort to change who they are."

The committee hearings continue.

stories.title: At a glance: Key proposals from Milburn's Neets report
stories.summary: A major review proposes widespread changes to help get young people into work across the UK.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The review has proposed widespread changes to tax, welfare, and education

Published 17 November 2026

A major review by former minister Alan Milburn has proposed widespread changes to help get young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neet) into work across the UK.

His report - which has now been published in full , external - says the UK should aim to reduce the rate of Neet young people from 13% to about 5% by 2036.

Its proposals relate mostly to England, with a recommendation that Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland adapt the principles to suit their own systems.

Here is a summary of the key points from the review:

Major report proposes welfare changes, apprenticeships and tax cuts to help 440,000 young people into work

Rights for young people

Young people should have a legal right to a route into education, training or work, and would be supported to do so under an "opportunity guarantee"

A new, locally-led Youth Opportunity Service in England would give young people one named advisor and a personalised participation plan - spelling out what action needs to be taken, by whom, and when

Tax, spending and other policy decisions should be put through a "youth opportunity test", to ensure they consider impact on younger generations

Schools

Prevention should start early, with primary and secondary schools required to identify and support pupils at risk of becoming Neet

Schools would also be required to offer work experience

A new performance measure would assess schools based on where their pupils end up

A new writing, numeracy and oracy check for pupils in Key Stage 3 (Years 7 to 9)

Colleges and apprenticeships

An extra 150,000 18- to 24-year-olds studying further education courses at colleges and other training providers each year

College funding to be based on how students perform and where they end up, rather than on how many students there are

A new digital open college, part-funded by employers and private investors, which would allow young people to study courses from colleges and universities

Aim to double the number of young people completing apprenticeships over the next decade - with more than a third of young people starting one every year

Where has the most jobs for 18-24 year-olds? Use our look-up to find out Published 18 hours ago

Watch: What's in the Milburn review? Published 19 hours ago

The young people caught up in Britain's Neets crisis Published 19 hours ago

Employers

An extra 170,000 job and apprenticeship opportunities to be created through employer incentives

Employers who take on any young person who has been Neet for six months should receive a £3,000 payment

Small businesses - with fewer than 50 employees - which do so should receive an extra £2,000

There would be an extra £2,000 payment if the young person has been in care or is disabled

Lower National Insurance costs for 21- to 24-year-olds, starting in retail and hospitality

Large employers should tell job applicants when they are unsuccessful

Mental health

Young people who are already Neet should have guaranteed access to fast-track services like talking therapies and counselling within three months

These should be accessible without a diagnosis

A new digital-first mental health care service should be the "starting point for young people to access help"

The government should introduce national maximum waiting times for young people's mental health care from 2028

Fitness to work, or "fit notes", to be issued through the new Youth Opportunity Service, rather than GPs

Why Milburn's Neets reforms will only save £200m a year by 2036 Published 18 hours ago

Welfare

An "entirely new benefits system" for under-25s

Young people to no longer get the health top-up of Universal Credit, which provides extra money for people whose health conditions limit their capacity to work

They would also no longer receive Personal Independence Payments (Pip), which help with the extra living costs of having a long-term health condition or disability

Instead, a new youth allowance would be set at the basic rate of Universal Credit for under-25s, with a higher rate for those living independently

A "local flexible health and disability fund" to be run by the local Youth Opportunity Service would pay for extra costs while a young person is receiving support

An additional cost allowance would replace Pip, providing "targeted financial support where disability-related extra costs are well established, significant and ongoing"

A new severe and complex needs insurance for those who will never be able to work

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Some firms are directing refunds to corporate leadership instead of reimbursing consumers, ProPublica finds

Several companies that received refunds for paying Donald Trump ’s tariffs have put those funds towards corporate bonuses instead of reimbursing consumers, an investigation from ProPublica has found.

After analyzing securities filings and earnings calls, ProPublica identified at least nine companies who said they were receiving tariff refunds and noted they were directing some of those funds to their leadership.

Stanley Black & Decker, a tool company that makes common household products including vacuums, electric drills and measuring tapes, told its consumers they were forced to raise prices because of Trump’s import fees, ProPublica reported. The company is expected to receive at least $298m in tariff reimbursements and indicated some of it will go to bonuses. Executives at TJ Maxx and Marshalls, discount department stores that are set to receive tariff refunds, also said the same.

A spokesperson for TJ Maxx and Marshalls, which are owned by the same TJX parent company, confirmed ProPublica’s reporting, and said that the company received an aggregate of $331m in refunds for a portion of the tariffs covered in the supreme court ruling. Because of these refunds, the company now had accrued “incremental expenses of $112 million for year-end incentive compensation and discretionary bonuses for eligible associates globally”, the spokesperson said.

“Given that this is an accrual, and we have not reached the end of our current fiscal year, we have not disclosed any breakout beyond this,” the company spokesperson said.

In financial disclosures, Stanley Black & Decker said the refund it received “was partially offset by directly attributable costs for variable incentive compensation”, according to ProPublica. Stanley Black & Decker did not immediately respond to request for comment.

The Trump administration has refunded at least $100bn to companies since August, about 60% of roughly $165bn in tariffs, after the supreme court ruled that Trump’s “liberation day” tariffs were illegal. The court ruled that the tariffs were unlawful because they overstepped his executive authority and should have required congressional approval.

Some companies immediately sued the US government for refunds after the ruling, though Trump signaled that he would “remember” which companies requested reimbursements and praised companies for holding off. The Trump administration has not specified which companies are receiving refunds, despite requests for information, according to ProPublica.

Though many companies said publicly that they had to increase prices because of tariffs, it has largely been unclear what companies are doing with their tariff refunds.

In its analysis, ProPublica found that almost all the companies that have publicly said they plan to use their tariff reimbursements to refund customers are those that deal directly with other businesses, rather than directly consumers. Some companies have remained “vague” about their plans for the reimbursements and have not specified whether those funds will go towards price decreases or holding back on future increases, according to the report.

Research has shown that US consumers have shouldered some of the cost of tariffs, with the New York Federal Reserve estimating that 26% of tariff increases pass through to consumer prices. The Yale Budget Lab estimated that tariffs cost households about $900 annually under current laws.

after newsletter promotion

Tariffs are one of several of Trump’s economic policies that have proven unpopular with voters, reflected in the widespread victories Democrats notched in the November midterms. A year after Trump’s tariffs were announced, a survey from the Pew Research Center found that 63% of Americans felt little or no confidence in his handling of tariffs.

Republican candidates across the country were largely punished for Trump’s tariffs and other White House decisions that have led to greater inflation. In the Associated Press’s November survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters, two-thirds said that Trump’s decisions had fueled inflation, while about half of 2022 midterm voters said the same thing about former president Joe Biden’s policies.

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Experts say US president may lean toward global affairs after domestic influence curtailed in midterm elections

Donald Trump is embarking on his first overseas trip since his Republican party’s thumping midterm repudiation by US voters, in what may herald a renewed focus on foreign policy for the remainder of his presidency.

The US president will meet his Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, for their first trilateral summit, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum in the Chinese city of Shenzhen. Before that, he will land in Manila in the Philippines on Tuesday for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit.

At the Asean summit, Trump is expected to sign a trade agreement with Thailand , push deals with other countries and lobby fellow leaders to favour the US over China on artificial intelligence.

He will also take part in the first leaders’ meeting of the Quad partnership – consisting of the US, Japan, India and Australia – since he returned to the White House in January 2025.

White House officials said the president would be accompanied to Apec by Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX entrepreneur who spent almost $500m (£380m) unsuccessfully supporting Republican candidates in this month’s midterms. The reason for Musk’s presence has not been explained.

The China leg of the trip will take place amid the continuing fallout from the Nvidia spying scandal , which prompted the company’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, to resign amid revelations he had had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Trump is under pressure to raise the matter with Xi when they hold a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of Apec.

The US president has said he does not plan to bring up the subject ; administration officials insist he will not do so and that the meeting will be dedicated to implementing a trade agreement between the two superpowers.

Huang persuaded the Trump administration to lift restrictions on the sale of Nvidia’s AI chips to China that had been imposed during Joe Biden’s presidency.

Mao Ning, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson, told reporters on Monday that at the trilateral summit, Xi, Trump and Putin “will exchange views in depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance”.

Some analysts have characterised the meeting as a “big three” gathering echoing the 1945 Yalta meeting of Winston Churchill, Franklin D Roosevelt and Joseph Stalin that in effect carved up postwar Europe, between a communist-ruled east and a democratic, capitalist west.

Such a prospect has alarmed Ukraine , which fears that Putin – who initially suggested the trilateral meeting – will use it to persuade Trump and Xi to agree to a settlement of the war with Russia on Moscow’s terms.

However, Trump has said Ukraine will not be up for debate at the meeting and that its main purpose will be to discuss ending the US’s war with Iran and “denuclearisation” – shorthand for a deal among the three powers to limit nuclear arms.

That is believed to be unpalatable to China , which has been increasing its nuclear arsenal, and has signalled an unwillingness to enter into reduction agreements until it is closer to parity with the US and Russia.

after newsletter promotion

Analysts say the main beneficiary of the three-way meeting is likely to be Putin, whose standing will be boosted by being treated on an equal footing by two other leaders whose countries are, in reality, much more powerful.

Expectations of a substantial agreement are low.

Lyle Goldstein, an international affairs fellow and China specialist at Brown University in the US, said the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting would not have a substantive result. “There will be no ‘Yalta’, as many have feared,” he said.

Jonathan Czin, the Michael Armacost chair in foreign policy studies at the Brookings Institution, said Trump’s lame duck status would deter Xi and Putin from trying to reach long-term arrangements with the US.

“Both men know Trump’s time is expiring even more quickly than his leverage – and that he will be irrelevant in a mere 26 months [when his term expires],” Czin told an online Brookings forum . “Why would either man make a deal with a leader whose time and leverage are waning? They will only do it if they think they can pilfer more from Trump diplomatically than they will be able to gain from the next American president.”

Nevertheless, Goldstein – who took soundings on Chinese expectations for the summit in a visit to Shenzhen last week – predicted Trump would follow the pattern of previous presidents by turning increasingly to global affairs while he faces the prospect of his influence on the domestic front being curtailed after the Democrats’ victories in the House of Representatives and the Senate.

“The president has been badly damaged by the election and will have limited prospects for the next two years,” he said. “That may cause him to be more active in foreign policy since he can act in that domain with fewer constraints. It would not surprise me if Trump is ready to go all-out to make some further splash in foreign policy.”

With the risks of reigniting the war with Iran high and the Russia-Ukraine war still resistant to a diplomatic resolution despite White House efforts, Goldstein suggested Trump could attempt “a dramatic foreign policy flourish in Asia”, such as an agreement with Kim Jong-un, the North Korean dictator with whom he has frequently boasted of having a close relationship. Kim is not expected to attend the Apec gathering, although there have been rumours he may appear.

October annual rate piles pressure on households as Iran war pushes up oil cost and rattles global economy

Inflation in the UK rose to 3.6% in October amid an increase in energy prices triggered by the war in the Middle East.

Figures from the Office for National Statistics show the headline rate of inflation as measured by the consumer prices index rose from 3.5% in September . City economists had forecast a reading of 3.6%.

As households brace for the colder winter months, the latest figures took into account a 4% increase in the Ofgem energy price cap from the start of October. Driven by rising wholesale gas prices, forecasters are warning of a further increase of as much as a quarter from January.

Andy Burnham’s government has pledged to offer support for households grappling with a fresh cost of living squeeze as the stop-start Iran conflict rattles the global economy and drives up inflation worldwide.

At the budget last month the chancellor, John Healey, announced plans for a £100 winter handout for 20 million households to cushion the blow from the global economic storm.

However, forecasters predict a further rise in inflation, with the Bank of England anticipating a peak of close to 5% next year.

Earlier this month Threadneedle Street raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4% and warned further increases in the cost of borrowing might be required to combat inflationary pressures unleashed by the Iran war.

Financial markets anticipate at least two quarter-point increases before the end of next year.

stories.title: Failed asylum seekers face removal without five-day notice period
stories.summary: Under proposed new rules, the Home Office would have six months in which to remove a person without telling them in advance.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 17 November 2026

The government is to change the law so that it no longer has to give failed asylum seekers notice before they are removed from the country.

Currently, people are given five working days' notice but ministers believe this leads to last-minute appeals which delay the process.

Under the new rules, once an asylum claim fails, the Home Office would have six months in which to remove the applicant without telling them in advance.

The move was criticised by the Refugee Council which said: "Removing people at such short notice will cause unnecessary distress and anxiety to people."

Imran Hussain, the director of the refugee charity, said: "The reality is that voluntary removals are far more effective at removing people than enforced returns.

"If you assist people to return with dignity, many will take that option, at far lower cost to the taxpayer."

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood will make the change by amending the Immigration and Asylum Bill which is currently going through Parliament.

The amendment will scrap the notice requirement for those who have exhausted the asylum appeals process.

Instead, the Home Office will have the power to remove people immediately, a power that will remain in place for up to six months.

The Home Office has not said how many additional people it thinks it will be able to remove but has pointed to Denmark where the number of migrants awaiting removal more than halved over five years to under 1,000 after a similar policy was introduced.

The previous government, led by Sir Keir Starmer, had pledged to clear the asylum backlog.

An asylum seeker is someone who wants to be in the UK because they say they cannot live safely in their own country due to persecution or violence.

The government must house an asylum seeker if they cannot financially support themselves while their claim is being considered. There were 89,089 people in asylum accommodation as of June 2026.

About 18% of those people, 16,021, were in hotels. These are used when there is not enough shared housing available, such as houses of multiple occupation (HMOs) or former military sites .

The government has pledged to stop the use of hotels by 2029.

More people are in hotels across the south of England than elsewhere in the UK, while HMOs are more common in the north of England and Scotland.
